for it is heard in such passages as, "The Vedas are his breath," and "From him the meters were born.
Alternatively, he is one for whom the true scriptures themselves are the source—that is, the cause of knowledge. To him...
Because of the scriptural hearing, "I ask you about the person known from the Upaniṣads," and because of the two-fold explanation given in the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*— where, in one view,

The prayer is: "May I have devotion toward Nṛsiṃha, the Man-Lion, and toward the one named Nṛsiṃha.

Here, there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) of either the identity between the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or the identity of the metaphor itself. The poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is *śleṣa* (punning paronomasia), and it pertains to both subjects under discussion.

For the word *vidvat* (learned) is shown in the *Triśatī* to refer to a devotee (*upāsaka*). "A *samaja* is a herd of animals; 'a *samaja* of animals, but a *samāja* of others,' so says Amara. (2)

This is also because of scriptural passages such as, "There the sun does not shine. It "conquers," meaning it exists with supreme excellence.

The meaning is that examples such as clay pots and the like are untenable. In this regard, the method of the system (tāntrika-prakriyā) is as follows:

in instances such as "I desire" or "I know," that very knowledge which is associated with the first-person singular (*uttama-puruṣa*), which persists through all manifestations (*sphuraṇa*), and which is designated as "light" (*prakāśa*), is Brahman. And that...

It is endowed with powers such as omniscience, universal sovereignty, universal agency, fullness, and pervasiveness. The manifestation of its very essence as bliss is supreme egoity (*parāhaṃtā*), which is supreme reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
She is designated by such terms as Lalitā Bhaṭṭārikā and Tripurasundarī. And it is stated in the *Viśvaśarīraskandha* of the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"Lordship, agency, autonomy, and the nature of consciousness [constitute her essence]."
Indeed, these are said by the wise to be synonyms for the notion of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā).

Thus [it is said]: because "this-ness" (idantā) does not manifest without "supreme I-ness" (parāhaṃtā), and because "I" and "this" stand in a relationship of mutual dependence, the visible object (dṛśya) which is accessible through the word "this" must be produced either by the power whose nature is "I-ness" or by Brahman as qualified by that [power]. And that visible object is indeed a transformation (pariṇāma) of that [power].

For, according to the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, "When that [power] has undergone transformation, no other [entity] is admitted," and because the natural force of such scriptural passages as "The modification is a mere verbal handle" applies precisely there;
there is absolute non-difference between power and the possessor of power, and between the material cause and its effect. It is not...

Furthermore, there is both difference and non-difference, as in the case of the followers of the Upaniṣads and others. For this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman" refers to non-difference, and not to sublation. All the scriptural texts concerning non-duality are likewise consistent precisely because they intend this [non-dual] perspective.

Since non-duality has been proclaimed by the Śruti—the crown of all means of valid knowledge—and by the Tantras that follow it, let it be that only the aspect of difference between cause and effect, which appears as contradictory to that [non-duality], is imagined; however, not the entire phenomenal world. "There is not the slightest diversity here."
In such scriptural passages as these, too, it is only the aspect of difference that is negated, not the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) itself.

Even the absence of the world, which appears to possess difference in statements such as "one only, without a second," is likewise occasioned solely by the absence of its qualifying attributes. For this very reason, in the *Bhāmatī*:

In the *Hāṭakamaṇimakuṭagrantha*, it is stated that difference (*bheda*) alone has an existence inferior to that of the gold, and not the crown; for it is necessary that a transformation (*pariṇāma*) must have an existence equal to that of the transforming substrate (*pariṇāmin*).
Likewise, in the passage "this duality is mere illusion" (*māyāmātram idaṃ dvaitam*), by the word "duality" (*dvaita*), it is indeed difference that is meant.
Falsity (mithyātva) is being stated; it does not, however, belong to that which possesses difference.

For if it were so, then just as the world possesses difference through the relation of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā), Brahman would also possess difference through the relation of sub-correlativity (anuyogitā). Consequently, absence could not be defined as that which is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.

Because there is no difference in their being established by logic, the consequence would be that [the world] is false. Consequently, it is established that even the Śruti accepts only the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda). Furthermore, the venerable Vyāsa also [established this] in the section beginning with "And [the world has] material cause, because of the non-contradiction of the proposition and the illustrative examples."

The theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is maintained by one who connects the proposition that all cognitions arise from a single cognition, the analogies of the clay pot and the nail-cutter, and the teaching on the desire "May I be many, may I procreate," and so forth.
This is precisely what was intended and explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras in the aphorism *ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt*.
Furthermore, even the Commentators, while explaining that very point in accordance with the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*),
[state] in the verse from the *Saundaryalaharī*, "Thou art the mind, thou art the ether," regarding Thee.
By the phrase "when [the cause] has transformed," his own preferred theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) is clearly elucidated. In this view,
the "falsity" (mithyātva) heard in the *Rahasyanāmasahasra* in passages such as "the substratum of the false world" refers to its being a form that is not distinct from itself.
There is impermanence in the form of the jar and so forth, and permanence in the form of Brahman;
even though there is no difference between the clay and the jar, there is destruction in the form of the jar, yet non-destruction in the form of the clay.
The exclusion of contradictory attributes and so forth should be inferred as in the case of [the term] *ceti* and others;

She consists of meaning (*arthamayī*), comprising the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) from Śiva down to the earth; she consists of sound (*śabdamayī*), comprising [the levels of speech] from Parā down to Vaikharī; she consists of the wheels (*cakramayī*), comprising [the centers of energy] from Bindu down to the Earth-palace (*bhūgṛha*); and she consists of the body (*dehamayī*).

Although in the *Tantrarāja* and other works, as well as in the *Saundaryalaharī*, the extraction of the *hādi-vidyā* alone is seen first, nevertheless, it is indeed the *Śrīvidyā* that is [the primary one] among the mantras there,
according to the statement: "Just as *parā* is [foremost] among the *kādi* [mantras]," and because it constitutes the essence of the *ṣoḍaśī*.

Because it possesses syllables that convey secret meanings— such as "even in a single syllable" and "the eleventh support"— and because of the great esteem accorded to this very [Triśatī] in the *Triśatī*, and because in the *Tripuropaniṣad* other [mantras] are extracted precisely on the basis of this [text] as their source.

The primacy of the Kādi-vidyā is established because the meanings taught in the *Yoginīhṛdaya* and other texts, as well as those that will be explained here, find their natural resonance (*svārasya*) precisely in this [vidyā], and because it was extracted first from the verse in the *Śāṅkhāyana-śruti* which begins, "Four carry him" (*catvāra īṃ bibhrati*).
Illuminating her countenance,
he addresses her with conventional terms such as "Desire," "The Womb," and "Lotus";
yet even the Vedic Puruṣa does not openly discourse upon that Vidyā.
Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, Guhā, Hasā, Mātariśvan, Abhra, Indra, again Guhā, Sakalā, and Māyā— this primordial knowledge (Ādividyā), the Mother of the Universe, is manifold.

Thus says the Śāṅkhāyana Śruti: the letter *ka* is Desire and Mātariśvan; the letter *e* is the Yoni; the fourth vowel (*ī*) is Kamalā; the letter *la* is Indra and Vajrapāṇi; and the two *guhas* (the syllables *huṃ-huṃ*) along with Māyā constitute the seed-syllable of Modesty (*lajjābīja*).

It laughs (*haseti*) and encompasses (*sakalati*) its own nature. Due to the compound with *guhā*, the plural number is used, and furthermore, the letter *sa* is not long. The same applies to the letter *la*. The letter *ha* is "cloud" (*abhra*). Through the use of such conventional (*sāṃketika*) terms, the necessity of extreme secrecy in the practice is established.
It comes to be. || 8 ||
He extracts the letters of the Vidyā: Krodhīśa mounted upon Śrīkaṇṭha, and Lakṣmī at the three corners;
Māṃsa mounted upon Anuttara—this is proclaimed as the first Vāgbhava-kūṭa. (9)
Śiva, Haṃsa, Brahmā, Viyat, and Śakra—each mounted upon a syllable;
this second peak is called Kāmarāja. (10)
This very third [syllable], liberated from Śiva and Vyoman, is indeed called the Peak of Power (śaktikūṭa).
The triad of Hṛllekhās should be joined at the end of each of the three peaks.

Krodhīśa and Brahmā are the letter *ka*. Śrīkaṇṭha and the unsurpassed syllable are the letter *a*. Mounted upon that [letter *ka*] means joined with it. The triangle is the womb (*yoni*). Lakṣmī is Kamalā. Flesh is Śakra, that is Indra. Śiva and space are the letter *ha*. Haṃsa.
The letter *sa*. Because it consists of a collection of syllables, it receives the designation "kūṭa" (peak/syllabic cluster). || 9-11 ||
The essential nature of Hṛllekhā consists of Vyoma, Agni, and Vāmalocanā; followed by Bindu, Ardhacandra, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, and Śakti.
Vyāpikā, Samanā, and Unmanā constitute the aggregate of twelve;
the collective totality of the nine [principles] beginning with Bindu is called Nāda. (13)
The sky is the letter *ha* alone, not qualified by the vowel *a*. Fire is the letter *ra* of that same kind.
The left eye is the letter *i*. The nine [points] beginning with the *bindu* are specific sounds to be articulated at times that are subtle, subtler, and most subtle.
Or rather, they are specific phonetic qualities (*varṇaviśeṣa*). Furthermore, unlike the letter *ka* and so forth, they are not clearly articulated;

they are heard as being similar to the notes on a lute string, and because they lack suffixes such as the *kāra*-suffix, the seed-syllables (*bīja*), the points (*bindu*), and the sounds (*dhvani*) are [designated] as "consisting of the planets" (*grahātmikā*) and so forth in the context of the three peaks (*trikūṭa*).
It should not be argued that the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and other such sounds lack the nature of a phoneme (*varṇatva*) simply because they are designated by the term *dhvani* in the Tantras;
for even though the aforementioned reasons apply to the *anusvāra*, *visarga*, and so forth, their status as phonemes is nonetheless accepted.
Otherwise, how could it be said that "sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are recognized in the system of Śumbhu"?

Having thus made this proposition, would the enumeration in the *Śikṣā*—“anusvāra and visarga”—be consistent? Nor does the lack of phonemic status (*varṇatva*) here follow merely from such a contradiction in number, because in that context only those [sounds] capable of being clearly articulated are counted. Nor...
It does not possess the nature of a phoneme (*varṇa*) because it is not manifested by the recognized locations such as the palate;
for that definition of non-manifestation-by-those-locations would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*), failing to apply to *paśyantī* and the other levels of speech.
Furthermore, the Vedic scripture stating, "Speech is measured in four quarters," clearly declares that a word (*pada*) consists of a collection of phonemes.

For this very reason, the description of the meaning of *nāda* (the sacred sound) in the *Catuḥśatīśāstra* is consistent. Nor can it be argued that its function as a reminder of the word-meaning is like the sound of a chariot; for in that case [of the chariot], there is a connection with the commencement of the *māhendra-stotra* by virtue of its being to be performed at that same time.

Since the status of being an object of recollection is established by scriptural statement (*vācanika*), the commonality of the sound of a chariot— which is shared by worldly sounds and others— lacks the capacity to cause recollection because it does not possess the power to do so;
however, in the present case, this is not the same, and thus there is a disparity.

By stating that there are fifteen syllables for each *hṛllekhā*— namely, the five consisting of the letters *ha*, *ra*, *e*, *anusvāra*, and *nāda*— in the passage beginning with "by the fifteen syllables produced from the three *hṛllekhās*," etc., [the number of syllables is established].
The conventional usage of the term "syllable" (*akṣara*) with respect to the *nāda* is found repeatedly in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"The ground, the moon, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhvan, Mādana,
the half-moon, and the bindu— these nine syllables are called Meru."
The mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru.

This is because such usage is seen repeatedly even in works like the *Jñānārṇava*. As for the usage of the term "dhvani," it should be understood either through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its similarity [to sound],
or through indication where the literal meaning is set aside (*neyārtha-lakṣaṇā*), since it is denotable by the word "sound" (*nāda*) as a synonym for *dhvani*.

Direction. And thus, since the first and third peaks consist of eighteen syllables each, while the middle peak consists of twenty-four, it is established that the Vidyā consists of fifty-eight syllables in total. This is so even though [the calculation] refers only to the eight [syllables] excluding the *bindu*.

In the science of mantras, there is no designation for *nāda*; nevertheless, it should be understood that for the sake of practical convenience, the [phonetic] sequence here is established as including those very [sounds]. || 12, 13 ||
He states what is already established:
"In the first [section], there are eighteen syllables; in the middle, there should be twenty-two syllables.
The last is equal to the first; by the total sum, there are fifty-eight. (14)
He states the duration of the phonemes: the Kāmakalā and the triangle are to be pronounced with two mātrās;
the hṛllekhā, devoid of the bindu, is to be pronounced with three mātrās. || 15 ||
The duration of other vowels is one and a half mātrās;
a bindu is half a mātrā, and each subsequent [vowel] is half the duration of the preceding one.
The duration of this *nāda* is the time of one and a half *mātrās*.

A *mātrā* is the duration of a short vowel; that of a long vowel is double that. For this very reason, *Kāmakalā*, *Kamalā*, the triangle (*trikoṇa*), and the womb (*yoni*) consist of two *mātrās*. [This applies] to the *Hṛllekhā*.
One *mātrā* for each of the two consonants, and two *mātrās* for the *kāmakaletā*, making three in total.
For the other ten syllables beginning with *ka*, which are accompanied by the vowel *a*, [there is one *mātrā* each]. Since the *bindu* is also a consonant, it has half a *mātrā*.

A short vowel should be known as having one measure (mātra), a long vowel is said to have two measures, and a protracted vowel (pluta) is to be understood as having three measures; a consonant, however, has half a measure.

Because of this statement: "Each subsequent [element] possesses the duration of each preceding one"—referring to the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the *rodhinī*, and so forth—the first half [of each] constitutes their respective durations:

the duration of the half-moon is that of the *rodhinī*, the duration of the *rodhinī* is that of the *nāda*, and so on in sequence. The intended meaning is as follows: a *lava* is a unit of time (*kālaparamāṇu*).
It is said:
"The time required for a fine needle to pierce through a cluster of lotus petals,
one petal at a time, is designated as a lava."
Therefore, O descendant of Bhṛgu, a time more subtle than that cannot be perceived.
According to this statement, one *mātrā* consists of two hundred and fifty-six *lavas*.
The *bindu* has one hundred and twenty-eight *lavas*; the *ardhacandra*, sixty-four;
the *rodhinī*, thirty-two; the *nāda*, sixteen; and the *nādānta*, eight.

There are four [units] of Śakti: two *lava*s for Vyāpikā, one *lava* for Samanā, but for Unmanā there is no time at all. Although in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, in the section on the conventions of the wheels (*cakrasaṃketa*), the time of the Bindu is stated by the phrase "having the form of a lamp and consisting of half a measure" (*dīpākāro 'rdhamātraśca*).
Having stated that the time of the [mandala] parts— ranging from the half-moon up to the Śakti—
is in the form of double portions, such as four parts, eight parts, sixteen parts, and so forth,
[it is taught that] the Śakti and the others possess a duration of time consisting of twice the number of parts of each preceding one.
It has been stated in general that there are sixty-four [units], and beyond that, they double and double again;
by that statement, the fifty-second part exceeding one hundred and twenty of the *mātrā* constitutes the nature of *unmanā*, which is the essential form of the *mātrā*.
It is understood that [the measure] consists of exactly five hundred and twelve *lava*s; for this very reason,

in the subsequent text where it says "beyond that, the supreme great [space] is unconditioned by space and time," the absence of temporal limitation is stated specifically as being beyond the *unmanā* state.
It is clearly perceived as such; nevertheless, regarding the verse "sixty-four," this refers to the sixty-fourth part of a *mātrā* of the *śakala*, and above that,
double that is the one hundred and twenty-eighth part of the *vyāpikā*, and double that again...

The meaning is that the portion of the *samanā* consists of two hundred and fifty-six units; this is clearly understood from the words "thereafter" (*tatastadūrdhvam*) and the two terms denoting "doubling. For this very reason, in the latter half [of the verse], there is a mention of the measure-portion of *śakti* and the others.

Regarding the passage "manonmanī tathā unmanī," the commentators Amṛtānanda and others have explained that the term *manonmanī*— which is a synonym for *samanā*— is intended to mean "up to and including *samanā*," thereby referring to the three levels beginning with *śakti*. [This applies] to *nāda*.
Of the nine [deities] beginning with Bindu. || 15, 16 ||
Eleven [syllables] are declared in the Vāk-kūṭa, and eleven and a half in the middle.
Seven and a half *mātrās* each, diminished by one *lava*, constitute the two powers;
taken together, these thirty-one *mātrās* of the mantra are reduced by three *lavas*.
In the third peak of Śakti. || 17-18 ||
Regarding the places of origin and the efforts [involved], he says:
"In the throat, in the throat and palate, in the palate, in the teeth, in the head, and in the nose;
through internal and external efforts such as contact and openness, there is the production of those phonemes. (19)
The three *ka* letters, the ten *a* letters, and the five *ha* letters are in the throat;

the second letter is in the throat and palate (*kaṇṭhatāluni*), being treated as a singular compound because it refers to parts of a living body; the four *ī* letters are in the palate; and the three *la* letters and two *sa* letters are in the teeth.
The three *repha*s are at the head; the ninefold triad beginning with the *bindu* is in the nose. Regarding "contacted" (*spṛṣṭā*):

the *ka*-letters are produced with the effort of contact (*spṛṣṭa-yatna*). The *a*-vowels are closed (*saṃvṛta*). The *ī*-vowels and the *e*-vowel are open (*vivṛta*). The *ra*-letters and *la*-letters are slightly contacted (*īṣat-spṛṣṭa*). The *ha*-letters and the two *sa*-letters [are likewise].
The *ceṣatvivṛta* (slightly open) [consonants] are [so called]; the *bindu* (anusvāra) and others are most closed (*saṃvṛtatama*). Such is the internal effort (*ābhyantara-yatna*).

The *ka*-letters are characterized by expansion (*vivāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), lack of voicing (*aghoṣa*), and weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*). The two *sa*-letters possess strong aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*) and are characterized by expansion and so forth. All vowels (*svarāḥ*) are acute (*udātta*).
The letters *ra* and *la* possess *saṃvāra*, *nāda*, *ghoṣa*, and *alpaprāṇa*. The letters *ha*, however, possess the triad beginning with *saṃvāra* as well as *mahāprāṇa*.
The *bindu* and others possess the fourfold set beginning with absolute *saṃvāra*. Thus is the external [classification].
Effort. || 19 ||
Now he describes the location, form, and shape of the phonemes:
"The first [phoneme], resembling the fire of universal dissolution, touches the *anāhata* [cakra] from the *mūlādhāra*;
from there, the second peak (*kūṭa*), which is the *ājñā*-cakra, shines like ten million suns. (20)
Therefore, one should meditate on the third [syllable] in the middle of the forehead, shining like ten million moons;
the phonemes should be visualized one above the other, like the gems of a garland.
The three locative phrases beginning with "from the *mūlādhāra*" (*mūlādhārāt*) are used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*;
the meaning is "starting from the *mūlādhāra*. Therefore, it means "starting from the *anāhata*" and "starting from the *ājñācakra*. And these are the three locations.

This refers specifically to the three *kūṭas* devoid of the *bindu* and so forth. At the root and the tip of the channel called *suṣumṇā*, there are two thousand-petaled lotuses; in between, thirty lotuses consisting of eight petals, six petals, and so on, have been explained in detail in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha* and other texts. Therein, above the anus...
Above two finger-breadths from the genitals, at the navel, heart, throat, and between the eyebrows,
are the six chakras known as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā, possessing four, six, ten, twelve, sixteen, and two petals respectively.
There are also six lotuses denoted by the term *cakra*, which are pressed between each pair of knots; this is explained in detail elsewhere. || 20, 21 ||
The sound arising from the *ādhāra* appears like a thread situated amidst the phonemes (*varṇa*).

Herein lies the process of the creation of sound: it possesses a subtle form of the creation of sound that is comparable to the subtle form of the banyan tree existing within the seed of a banyan tree.

Tripurasundarī, whose nature has been previously described, is precisely that which is denoted by the term "Parā," based on the etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*) of possessing such a subtle form. And she alone is called *Mātṛkā* through the etymological derivations: she measures (*māti*), she transcends (*tarati*), and she embodies (*kāyati*). And in her—

Even though She is changeless, by the power of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of beginninglessly established living beings, the desire to emit the universe—which was previously withdrawn within Herself—arises. Thereupon, She contemplates the objects to be created, according to the Vedic scripture:
"She thought, 'May I become many; may I procreate. Such a contemplation alone is [the cause].

Taking that as the ground for its application, the term "Paśyantī" is employed for her. And she herself, known as Mātṛkā Paśyantī, is called "Utterly Transcendent" (uttīrṇā) because she has transcended the path of the instruments [of speech].
Her constituent parts—the eight powers beginning with Vāmā and so forth—have been explained in detail elsewhere. Therefore:

That very [power] is ninefold by way of its individual (vyaṣṭi) and collective (samaṣṭi) aspects. From that, the nine nādas—beginning with the unmodified void (avikṛta-śūnya) and so forth—are born. And their collective totality, which is designated by such terms as "the path of nāda" (nādadhvan), is neither too subtle like Parā nor too gross like Vaikharī; therefore, it is called Madhyamā.

The *mātṛkā* consists of the form of the middle constituent; through the unmodified touch of emptiness (*śūnya*), it is the ninefold resonance (*nāda-navaka*) known as *bindu*, *śakti*, and the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*), which resides in the six centers beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, as well as in the *nāda*, the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*), and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Through the nine sounds— corresponding to the nine groups beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*— the Mātṛkā known as Vaikharī is born; indeed (*vai*), because it is most clearly manifest, she reaches (*rāti*) the sense of hearing, which is of the nature of space (*kham*) residing within the cavity of the ear.
The detailed explanation of this is found elsewhere, starting with the etymological derivation: "it becomes the object of the cognition produced by that.

And thus, since properties of letters such as *katva* (the quality of being the letter *ka*) and properties of sounds such as *ṣaḍjatva* (the quality of being the note *ṣaḍja*) are experienced in the letter *ka* and so forth, there is a persistence of the transformer within the transformation—just as in the case of clay and a jar.

And because it is perceived within the phonemes (*varṇa*), the *nāda* is interwoven through them. Just as a specific cloth produced from specific threads is denoted by the word *varṇaka*, here the suffix *-ka* is omitted;
thus, the term *varṇa*—which primarily denotes a syllable—is used in a double sense (*śleṣa*) to refer to the phoneme. It is like a quality (*guṇa*).

The meaning is: like a specific thread that serves as the material cause for a particular cloth called "colored," and like the string that supports the jewels in a garland. Regarding the phrase "situated in the midst of the letters," the meaning is: situated in the middle portion between two letters, and within the body of the letters.
The meaning is this: within the interval between two phonemes,
there is the manifestation of the pure *nāda*, like a pure thread situated in the middle of two jewels,
within the interior of the body of the phoneme.

However, due to the non-difference of those respective phonemes (*varṇa*), the resonance (*nāda*) appears as if woven together like threads in a cloth, or like clay within a jar; it is not, however, the case that the analogy of a thread inside a gem applies here, because that [thread] is entirely distinct from the gem. || 21 ||
Now he describes the location, form, and appearance of the remaining nine, beginning with the *bindu*:
"In the center, the *bindu* shines like a lamp, circular in shape. (22)
Above that is the semicircle (ardhacandra), so named because of its shape and luster;
then above that is the Rodhinī, triangular in form and possessing the brilliance of moonlight.
The *nāda* is like a vein situated between two stalks resembling rubies;
the end of the *nāda* has the luster of lightning and is like a ploughshare joined with a dot on its left side.
In the two horizontal dots, Śakti has the form of a channel rising from the left;
Vyāpikā is said to bear the form of a triangle arising from the dots.
Samanā has the form of a line joined with two dots above and below;
that same [line], when devoid of the upper dot, is Unmanā, and above that is Mahābindu.
The body of Śakti and the others, however, has the luster of a mass of rays from twelve suns.
"In the middle of the forehead" (madhyephālam) means within the forehead; the compound is formed according to the rule *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*. It is thus descriptive of its radiance and form.

The meaning is that its luster is like a half-moon and its shape is likewise. The two dots (*bindu*) representing the testicles and the central line representing the spinal cord—these three combined constitute the form of *nāda*. Between the two dots is a staff-like form resembling a tail, radiant as a jewel.

This is because it is stated in the *Cakrasaṃketokti*. The term *śeva* refers to the channel (*nāḍī*) situated between the two testicles; however, the traditional interpretation is that the *maṇi* is a ruby (*padmarāga*). The qualification of the staff (*daṇḍa*) as being in the form of the *śeva* is intended to exclude solidity and rigidity.

The interpretation that [the term] *śeva* is used because it refers to preparations of flour mixed with hair-like strands (*keśatulyapiṣṭavikāra*) when consumed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is not at all contradictory. [Furthermore,] the plow has its tip pointing upward and its handle to the right, while there is a dot (*bindu*) on the left side; this is the form of the end of the *nāda*. Like the *visarjanīya*, [it is] above and below.
To dispel the misconception that there are two dots (*bindu*), he says "diagonally" (*tiryak*).

The meaning is that it has the form of a channel-line (*sirā-rekhā*) which, starting from the left dot located in the left portion, moves upward and emerges. Thus, Śakti has the form of a channel-line arising from the left dot.
In the *Cakrasaṃketanirṇaya*, because it is the word of a seer (*ārṣa*), the entire term *bindu-pada* is construed with the preceding word as a member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound,
and also with the following word as a member of a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound, according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣi-nyāya*).

This is because of the explanation provided by the traditional commentators (*sāṃpradāyika*). Although the word *udyat* is a general term, it is used here with a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer specifically to [the channel] arising from the *bindu*. Thus, one should analyze the compound as "that whose form is like a vessel (*sirā*) arising from the *bindu* located on the left," precisely by virtue of the qualification that the *bindu* is situated on the left.

In the commentary, there is no difficulty whatsoever in explaining that "in the southern direction, there is understood to be a single drop (bindu) devoid of channels. Furthermore, the Vyāpikā is triangular in shape with its apex touched by the drop;
it consists of a straight line situated between two drops. This is stated in the passage beginning with the word "Samanā."

Lest two dots, like the [two] *śaktis*, be positioned horizontally, he says "above and below" (*ūrdhvādhaḥ*), following the oral tradition. They are "joined" (*saṃyutā*)—meaning they are fused at their upper and lower parts—and not situated without touching one another. And this...
She is situated at the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā). She is also designated as *manonmanī*.
Because it is easy to achieve the emergence of a mental state reaching this far through a specific practice of the mind itself in its unobstructed form, she is called *samanā*.

But above this, the state of *unmanā* arises because the mind, having attained another form (*rūpāntara*), becomes the object of stability; thus, due to the mind having transcended [its ordinary state], it is *unmanā*.
Although the station above *unmanā* is not directly relevant to the present context, it belongs to the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*).

In connection with the partless meditation (*niṣkalabhāvanā*) included within the threefold meditation, he says—by way of incidental discussion—"Beyond that is the Great Bindu" (*tadūrdhvaṃ mahābinduḥ*). Regarding "of Śakti and the others":
according to the tradition, this refers to the three ending with Samanā; [that is,] of the three beginning with Śakti.

The reading "tanavaḥ" (bodies) is appropriate [in the sense of] "having a splendor equal to twelve suns. The detailed expansion of the limbs, whose nature consists of the *bindu* and other [phonemes], is to be seen in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*. (22–26)
Now he describes the manner of pronouncing the phonemes:
"Having thus understood the place [of articulation] of the phonemes, one should pronounce them with effort. (27)
The first *nāda* should be uttered together with the second *kūṭa*;
one should utter the second *nāda* with the third [kūṭa], not separately.
By merging these two— the *bindu* and so forth, and the ninefold [syllables]— which reside within the previous *kūṭa*s, one should contemplate the variegated third *kūṭa*.
One should utter the third [syllable] in sequence, beginning with the *bindu* and ending with *samanā*;
one should contemplate this as being dissolved within the *unmanī*, for such is its utterance.

The "place" (*sthāna*) refers to the sites of production such as the throat and the sites of abiding such as the *mūlādhāra*. "With effort" (*yatnāt*) means preceded by internal and external exertion. This, moreover, pertains to matters other than mental recitation (*mānasajapa*). In that regard, there is the visualization of the respective places and efforts.
It should be understood that this is the application of the *mātra*. The *nāda* consists of the ninefold group beginning with the *bindu*.
Since each preceding *kūṭastha-nāda* is essentially already uttered through the pronunciation of each subsequent *kūṭa*, no separate effort or delay in time need be made regarding it.

This is the meaning. Regarding the third peak (kūṭa), however, since there is no subsequent peak, both [the preceding and the following] are required; thus he says, "beginning with the bindu" (bindvādika). || 27–30 ||
Previously, the duration of the nature of the Vidyā was stated; now, having extracted the time for its recitation, he says:
"Ten in the first [part], those same [ten] with a half in the middle, and eight in the third peak."
The time for the recitation of the Manu-mantra consists of twenty-nine measures minus one *ekalava*. || 31 ||

In the first peak (kūṭa) there are ten morae; in the middle, the Kāmarāja peak, those same ten and a half morae; and in the third peak, eight. The two preceding and following phrases of this [verse] are to be applied twice each, according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (kākākṣinyāya). By that, they are reduced by one unit.

The meaning is that seven and a half *mātrās* remain as they were previously situated in the third peak (*kūṭa*). Summing them up, he says "minus one *lava*," which means twenty-nine [mātrās] in the case of vocal recitation (*vācika*).
However, the aforementioned durations and so forth do not apply to mental recitation (*mānasa*). As for those situated in the first and second peaks, wherever [they may be]:

It should be understood that in the case of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, as well as in the individual recitation of each single *kūṭa* syllable as a constituent part of the twilight rites (*sandhyā*), the rules for the application (*viniyoga*) of the *kūṭas* are meaningful only when they are uttered individually. || 31 ||
Now, he describes the specific natures of the *kūṭas*, which are divided into four types according to the distinction between individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*):
"Due to the division into individual and collective, there are four seed-syllables (*bīja*) in this [mantra]."
The forms of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the inexpressible are to be meditated upon. || 32 ||

These four seed-syllables (bījas) should be meditated upon as the various forms of the following: the fire-pit (puṭadhāman), the reality (tattva), the seat (pīṭha), the lineage (anvaya), the linga, the Mothers (mātṛs), and their collective totality (tatsamaṣṭi). || 33 ||

The *anākhyā* (the Inexplicable) is the synthesis of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*), or rather, it is a specific state of abiding characterized by indifference even toward the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*).
The sixfold group beginning with the *puṭas* and the sevenfold group of abodes (*dhāmas*) each consist of three forms individually.

The collective totality (*tatsamaṣṭi*) of each one is thus fourfold—namely, the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and their state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*). The abodes (*dhāmāni*) are seven, consisting of the nature of the Lord of the Wheel (*cakranātha*), the ten energies (*daśa-śakti*), and the triad of selves (*ātmatraya*). Among these:

The wheels (cakras) are the fire-wheel, the sun-wheel, the moon-wheel, and the Brahma-wheel. The lords (nāthas) are Mitreśanātha, Ṣaṣṭhīśanātha, Uḍḍīśanātha, and Caryānandanātha. The states (daśās) are waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turīyā). The powers (śaktis)—
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śāntā, Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Ambikā, Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Mahātripurasundarī; and the Self (Ātman),
the Inner Self (Antarātman), the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the Gnosis-Self (Jñānātman).

The principles (tattvas) are the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), and the principle of all (sarvatattva). The sacred seats (pīṭhas) are Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and the seat of Oḍyāṇa. The lineages (anvayas) are the eastern, southern, western, and northern lineages; these alone [are they].

The signs— whether self-manifested (*svayaṃbhū*), produced by effort (*bāṇa*), or otherwise— and the supreme [sign] are described by means of the term "pledge" (*samaya*) and the term "tradition" (*āmnāya*). The matrices (*mātṛkā*)— namely *paśyantī*,
*madhyamā*, *vaikharī*, and *parā*— are spoken of as the referents of the term "abode" (*dhāma*).
The meaning of the word "mātṛ" (mother) is the triad of powers. || 32, 33 ||

Now he states the essential nature of each individual syllable: "In each single action, which is threefold due to the distinctions of emanation (sṛṣṭi) and so forth, Brahmā and the others are the presiding lords, accompanied by their own powers such as Bhāratī and the rest. (34)

These three, beginning with Brahmā, and these three Śaktis, beginning with Bhāratī, are the very nature of each individual syllable, according to the method that will be explained in the section on the Śākta meaning. (35)

The activity of creation (*sṛṣṭikarma*) is threefold: the creation of creation (*sṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), the maintenance of creation (*sṛṣṭisthiti*), and the dissolution of creation (*sṛṣṭisaṃhṛti*). Likewise, the activity of maintenance (*sthitikarma*) consists of the creation of maintenance (*sthitisthiti*), the maintenance of maintenance (*sthitisthiti*), and the dissolution of maintenance (*sthitisaṃhṛti*). Similarly, the activity of dissolution (*saṃhṛtikarma*) also includes the creation of dissolution (*saṃhṛtisṛṣṭi*).

[The stages are] withdrawal-stability, and withdrawal-withdrawal. Here, for each triad, the three [deities] beginning with Brahmā—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—together with Bhāratī, Pṛthivī, and Rudrāṇī, are the presiding deities.
And thus, in the first *kūṭa*, the letter *ka* is indeed another form of Brahmā, while the triangle is...
The fourth vowel is the nature of Bhāratī; the letter *la* is the nature of Viṣṇu;
the letter *ha* is the nature of Rudra; the letter *ra* is the nature of Rudrāṇī;
and the fourth vowel is the nature of the couple consisting of Śāntā and Ambikā. In the second *kūṭa*:
Having abandoned the letter *ha* from the middle [kūṭa], this same method applies to the remaining syllables.
However, in the third *kūṭa*, because the *ha* abandoned in the second *kūṭa* is of the nature of Brahman, the sequence begins with the letter *sa* starting from Bhāratī herself.
The power (śakti) is mentioned first because it is predominant as the peak-syllable (kūṭa) of power.
This very point he expresses [in the verse]: "by that which will be explained regarding the meaning of Śākta. (34, 35)

Now, he describes the nature of the remaining [elements], the *bindu* and so forth: "The *nādas*, arising from the *kuṇḍalinī* known as *hṛllekhā*, *kāmakalā*, and *aparārdhakalā*, should be contemplated as consisting of the triad of triads of *cakras*. (36)
Here, within the first *kūṭa*, that which is the *hṛllekhā*—and within that, the *kāmakalā*—is the *kalā* beyond the supreme (*parārdha*) which is to be known solely through the mouth of the Guru;
she is called the *vahnikuṇḍalinī*. That very same [energy] is the *sūryakuṇḍalinī* in the second *kūṭa*.

In the third peak (kūṭa), she is called Somakuṇḍalinī. Nāda, which is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of Bindu and the other [phonemes], has arisen from that very source, like a line of soot on the wick at the tip of a lamp flame. Thus, it has risen starting from the Unstruck (anāhata).

The *nāda*— the other form of the three wheels (*cakras*) consisting of the Trailokyamohana, Sarvāśāparipūraka, and Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, which are of the nature of the threefold emanation— is that *nāda* which,
having arisen starting from the middle of the eyebrows, bestows all good fortune.
The other form of the three wheels— which accomplish all aims, provide all protection, and exist in a threefold manner— consists of the *nāda* arising from the location of the *bindu*,
[which is] the three wheels consisting of all bliss, which remove all diseases and bestow all accomplishments.
These should be meditated upon as the other form of that which consists of the three forms of withdrawal. || 36 ||
Now, he explains that the five states (*avasthā*), the six voids (*śūnya*), and the seven equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) should be visualized at the time of recitation,
by means of sixteen verses beginning with "the ten sense organs" and ending with "thus the state."
The waking state consists of the functioning of the ten sense organs;
therein, the cause in the form of light is to be meditated upon in the third letter, *ra*.
The five organs of action— speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ— and the five organs of knowledge— the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears:
the functioning of these ten in producing their respective objects is worldly activity (vyavahāra), and that indeed is the waking state.

In that context, the knowledge whose nature is the cause, being formless, should be meditated upon during the stage of contemplation as having the nature of light, in the place of the letter *ra* within the third peak (*kūṭa*). || 37 ||
The functioning of the fourfold internal organ is the dream state;
it should be understood as arising from the third letter 'Ā', yet it is to be contemplated in the region of the throat. (38)

The mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*) are the four internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Through these alone, the dream state functions. Its generator, the Light, is to be understood as the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*) residing within the third *hṛllekhā*. Furthermore, it is located in the region of the throat.
It should be considered as a compound consisting of two members; the analysis of the compound is: "that which resides in the throat (galastha) and is the letter *la* (la). || 38 ||

The experience of the individual soul (jīva), which has become almost dissolved due to the dissolution of internal mental activity—that indeed is to be understood as deep sleep (suṣupti) in the Third Bindu. 39.

According to the Vivaraṇa school, three modifications (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*)—having as their objects the Self, happiness, and nescience—are accepted; therefore, he says "of the internal modification" (*āntaravṛtteḥ*).
This means: of the modification in the form of a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). [This refers to] the Vārtika school.
Deep sleep is precisely the total absence of the functioning [of the mind]; it occurs at the third point, located in the forehead. || 39 ||
The experience of the sound that manifests consciousness is said to be the fourth state (turyāvasthā).
Its contemplation should be performed by pervading the triad beginning with the half-moon (ardhacandra) and so forth. 40.
The manifestation of the fourth state (*turya-avasthā*), which pervades the *ardhacandra*, *rodhinī*, and *nāda*, should be contemplated.

(40) That state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta-avasthā*), which is a single mass of bliss inaccessible even to the speech of men, should be contemplated within the pentad beginning with the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*). (41)
Having examined the five states, he now examines the six voids:
"In the third position, at the place of the letter *ra*, at the *bindu*, and at the *rodhinī*, as well as at the *nādānta* and the *vyāpikā*, there are five voids resembling the moon. (42)
In the state of *unmanī*, one should contemplate the formless sixth [element], the great void (*mahāśūnya*).
The moon-moon is the void in the shape of a crescent moon located at the tip of a peacock feather.
This has been stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
For one meditating on the fivefold emptiness through mandalas with variegated forms like the feathers of a peacock,
the supreme void— the highest ether— becomes his very body.
Thus it is said: "O fair-faced one, O beloved, having left aside three by three at the twelve locations beginning with Agni,
one should know the three voids (śūnya) as being separated by single intervals."
Beyond the three voids, in the supreme state, one should contemplate the great void.
Thus, in the convention of worship (*pūjā-saṃketa*), among the twelve locations beginning with the letter *ra* and ending with the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*),

one should understand that by omitting three [locations] at a time, there is a triad of voids (*śūnya-traya*) situated in the middle, each separated by one; this refers, by implication, to the Half-moon (*ardhacandra*), Power (*śakti*), and the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*).

The meaning is that there are three voids (śūnya) above that, which constitutes the fourth. Alternatively, having omitted three at the beginning and three at the end, within the middle group of six— beginning with the half-moon and ending with Vyāpin— one void follows each after a single interval.

Although the meaning is clearly understood as "the fourth" refers to the three voids within the half-moon, the resonance (nāda), and the power (śakti), while the pervasive one (vyāpikā) is the great void (mahāśūnya)— nevertheless, O Sovereign of the Gods, there is a group of six voids and again the five states (avasthā).
Meditating with the mind upon the sevenfold form of the equinox, one should recite the mantra.

Because this would contradict the initial statement, the meaning must be otherwise. For instance, the word *agnyādi* (fire, etc. is a separate term that connects with the "three voids" (*śūnyatraya*). The word *anta* (end) denotes the final constituent part;
thus, by implication, it refers to the twelve constituent parts associated with the final *hṛllekhā*.

One should understand that within the sequence beginning with the letter *ha* and ending with *unmanā*, starting from the fire-syllable *ra* and extending through the two voids, there is a triad of voids, which constitutes the "sixfold void. And this does not occur through a continuous succession starting from *ra*, but rather with each one separated by an interval; therefore, he says: "separated by single intervals. This refers to the first void.

When it is stated that [the letter *ra*] occupies the place of the *repha*, it follows by implication that there is an intervention by six [factors]: the letter *ha*, the vowel *i*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the resonance (*nāda*), power (*śakti*), and *samanā*. This very point is expressed by the words "three by three."
The meaning is "having left behind three doubled [units]. From the "three voids" (*śūnyatrayāt*) means from the triad of voids;

that is, from that group of six. The form *supām* is derived from the *su*-class of case endings; here, the *ṅas* ending has been replaced by *ād*. The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).
Among those, the last one—the final—is the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*) in the state of *unmanī*.
It should be understood that this was stated with such difficulty because the thorough cultivation of this [meditation] is the supreme secret.
He states the seven equinoxes attained in succession:
"The conjunction of the vital breath, the self, and the mind is called the 'vital equinox' (prāṇaviṣuva). (43)

The wind whose essence is the letter *ka* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Some maintain that the unity of these—the self, the vital breath, and the mind—is designated as the "equinox of the vital breath" (*prāṇaviṣuva*). Others follow the literal meaning of the text. —43‖
He describes the equinox of mantra (mantraviṣuva):

"In the initial peak-syllable and resonance, from the unstruck sound (anāhata) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), through the division of individual and collective [aspects], and of one's own fourfold seed-syllables. (44)
The contemplation of oneness through the state of being composed of sound (*nāda*) is called the "equinox of mantra" (*mantraviṣuva*).

This consists of the unification of the four seed-syllables within the sound of the initial peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), as well as the unification of one's own self with the sound arising from the foundational support (*ādhāra*).
It is not [merely] the unification of the self with the sound arising from the foundational support.
Together with the primordial [sound] that has begun from the Unstruck (anāhata),
having realized the form of the Self dissolved within the sound arisen from the Foundation (ādhāra)—
through the conjunction and separation of the syllables of the mantra, O Maheśvarī!
The contemplation of the nature of sound (nāda), from the unstruck (anāhata) up to the end of the support (ādhāra),
is the equinox (viṣuva).

Thus, from the statement of the Kādimatīya school: "By conjunction" means by way of the totality (samaṣṭi); "by disjunction" means by way of the individuality (vyaṣṭi)—the word "of the fourfold [elements]" is to be supplied as the remainder. "The end of the supports" refers to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Thus, it is called "the end of the end of the supports."

They explain [the text] by means of the tantra [method], because the two final words exist, taking it to mean "up to the aperture of Brahmā" (*brahmarandhrāntam*). However, if the prefix *āṅ* is elided so as to mean "from the base up to the end" (*ā ādhārāntāt*), then everything is perfectly consistent.
He now states the equinox of the channels (*nāḍīviṣuva*):
From the upward movement of the sound arising from the base, it reaches as far as the aperture of Brahmā. || 45 ||
Piercing the twelve knots of the six cakras by way of the suṣumṇā alone, the conjunction of the channels, sounds, and phonemes is the "equinox of the channels" (nāḍikā-viṣuva). || 46 ||

There are twelve knots, with one knot each below and above the six cakras beginning with the Mūlādhāra. It is precisely by way of piercing those knots that the Suṣumṇā nāḍī extends from the Mūlādhāra to the Brahmarandhra. By that very path, [the sound] of Nāda...
The meaning is that the pronunciation of the sequence of phonemes through meditation on their connection with the channels (nāḍī) is called the "equinox of the channels" (nāḍī-viṣuva). —45, 46.
He describes the perfectly tranquil equinox (praśāntaviṣuva):

Within the letter *ra*, which is the syllable of the *kāmakalā*, and within the digit of the heart (*hārdakalā*) beginning with the point (*bindu*), the sound (*nāda*) arises there, becoming increasingly subtle until it reaches the end of sound (*nādānta*). (47)
The meditation on its dissolution within the *śakti* is declared to be the state known as *praśāntaviṣuva*.

This is the stage of extreme subtlety of the *nāda*— which begins from the *ādhāra* and proceeds through the seven locations beginning with the letter *ra* in the third *kūṭa*— in the successive moments following the impact.
Like the sound of a bronze cymbal; the meaning is that its dissolution should be brought about within that power (śakti). || 47, 47- ||
He describes the equinox of Śakti:
"One should contemplate the Nāda, which has entered into Śakti, as dissolved within Samanā. (48)

The meaning is that the "equinox of power" (śaktiviṣuva) refers to the dissolution of the most subtle *nāda*, which has been revived again from the station of *śakti*, after it has transcended the *vyāpikā* and reached *samanā*. || 48 ||
Furthermore, he states that the dissolution of the extremely subtle *nāda*, which has been revived following *samanā*, into *unmanā* is the "equinox of time" (*kālaviṣuva*):
"These two, having reached *unmanā*, are called the power-equinox (*śaktiviṣuva*) and the time-equinox (*kālaviṣuva*)."
He states the equinox of reality (*tattvaviṣuva*):
"In the constituent parts of the *śrīvidyā*-kūṭa, beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *unmanā*. (49)
In all [the levels] situated within the region from Akula up to Unmanā,
[the duration is] three hundred and seventeen *truṭis*, plus one and a half *nimeṣas*.
When the sound has been uttered, at its conclusion there occurs the realization of reality;
this very cause for the manifestation of consciousness is known as the Equinox of Reality (tattvaviṣuva). || 51 ||
Among the thirty-two lotuses mentioned, the two at the bottom and the final one are *akula* lotuses;
the remaining ones are *kula* lotuses. Although the initiation of the letters of the *vidyā* proceeds from the *kula* lotus called the *mūlādhāra*, nevertheless, [this is so] of the *cakrarāja*.
Since it is stated in the *Catuḥśatikā*— beginning with the words "starting from the thousand-petaled lotus below that which is called Sakala, in Akula, and in that which is named Viṣu"—
that the Śrīvidyā also begins from that point by way of the non-difference between the Kula and Akula Vidyās, so it is taught in the Tantras.

"Adhyuṣṭa" means three and a half. A "nimeṣa" is the duration of a blink of the eye. One three-thousandth part of that is a "triṭi"—the time it takes for the eye to blink when a healthy man is sitting at rest.
The thirtieth part of that is proclaimed as a *tatpara*;
and a hundredth part of a *tatpara* is designated as a *truṭi*.
According to this statement,

when the utterance of the *nāda* is performed in such a manner— preceded by its connection to the positions of the constituent parts of the *vidyā* for a duration of seventeen hundred and eight thousand *truṭis*— then:
The realization of reality as non-different from one's own consciousness occurs; this very utterance is the equinox of reality (*tattvaviṣuva*). —49–51—
He defines *japa* (recitation) by means of a concluding summary:
"Thus, for one who remembers the five, six, seven, and nine wheels—which are the equinoxes devoid of states—as well as the objects of the mind, the utterance of the syllables is indeed *japa*. (52)
The fourfold number is sequentially associated with the four states and so forth.

The contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the three *nādas* as being the nature of the three wheels has been explained previously. However, in the *Cakrasaṃketanirūpaṇa*, another triad is also mentioned: the threefold contemplation of the wheel, which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).

Regarding the "with parts" (*sakala*) and "without parts" (*niṣkala*): the contemplation of the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana within the nine locations— the thousand-spoked wheel of *Akula*, the five [centers] beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, the subtle tongue, the space between the eyebrows, and the station of the *bindu*— is the "with parts."

The second [stage] is the contemplation of that [reality] from the *bindu* up to the *unmanī*; the third is the contemplation of it within the *mahābindu* alone. This occurs for one who does not attend to the meanings of the mind or the mantra, but [focuses instead] upon the fifty-eight syllables (*varṇas*) of the *vidyā*.

The meaning is that the recitation— what is denoted by the term *japa*— consists of the utterance of the remaining forty syllables, after the removal of the two initial *kūṭas*, the two groups of nine [syllables] beginning with the *bindu*, and so forth.
Through the power of his Guru’s compassion, Bhāskararāya has brought to completion the first part of this most secret Varivasyā. (53)

Thus ends the first part of the *Varivasyārahasya* and its commentary, the *Tatprakāśa*, composed by Bhāsurānandanātha, who is also known by the name Bhāskararāya and is a worshipper at the feet of the venerable Nṛsiṃhānandanātha.
The second part: that which is studied as a constituent of the body of recitation (japa), being uncomprehended, is uttered merely by vocal intonation (nigada).
Like dry fuel in a fireless place, it never blazes forth at all.
He states that knowledge of the meaning is necessary because of the reproach of uttering words devoid of knowledge of their meaning, and because sin is inferred from such an act:
"The utterance of a word devoid of knowledge of its meaning bears no fruit."
An oblation cast into ashes devoid of fire does not blaze. || 54 ||
For those who do not understand the meaning and merely recite various kinds of words,
the donkey is the only fitting object of comparison for one who carries a load of sandalwood.

The donkey is "possessed of wheels" (cakrīvān). Although, as in the Vedic passage "the donkey carrying a load of sandalwood," the donkey alone serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), nevertheless,
only that which possesses a greater degree of the quality that determines similarity can function as the standard of comparison.
In order to suggest that superiority, there is an inversion of the standard roles of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, as in the figure of speech *pratīpa*. (54, 55)
Objects of value must be thoroughly understood by those who do not desire mere human ends; for those who show no regard for such objects, there is no gain at all, but rather misfortune.
By this, the eternality of the knowledge of the meaning is stated. || 56 ||
And those meanings, spoken by Śiva, are of various kinds according to the different classes of Tantras and Upaniṣads. Desiring to collect them, he indicates [the subject matter] as follows:
"Now, therefore, the first meaning to be expounded is that of the Pūrṇagāyatrī."
The meaning of the essential nature, the meaning of the tradition, and the fourth, the innermost secret meaning. || 57 ||
The Kaulika meaning, the secret meaning, and the meaning of the Great Principle;
the meaning of the name, the meaning of the form of the word, and the meaning residing in a single part of the name. (58)

The meaning of power (śakti), the meaning of equanimity (sāmarasya), the meanings of all things endowed with qualities, and the meaning of the Great Saying (mahāvākya)—these are the meanings of the *Pañcadaśī*, commensurate with itself. (59)

Immediately thereafter—because, as stated above, knowledge of the meaning is indispensable—the meanings are now being explained; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Of the complete Gāyatrī together with its fourth quarter: "its own" means its constituent syllables (*varṇa*); "equalized by them" means having a number identical to that count.

"Up to fifteen," so it is said. Alternatively, in the section concerning the meaning of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), thirty-seven phonemes will be clarified in the *Kādividyā*; the meaning is that there are an equal number of topics corresponding to them. (57–59)
He states the meaning of the Gāyatrī as set forth in the Tripuropaniṣad: "He desires" (kāmayate)—that *ka* is desire; that is the meaning of the word *brahma*.
"Of Savitṛ, the most excellent" (*saviturvareṇyam*)—this is the meaning of the second syllable, referring to the supreme excellence of Savitṛ. (60)
The fourth meaning is the *dhīti* (splendor) of the God who dwells within all as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*).
The syllable *la*, representing the earth (*pṛthvī*) or the great ground (*mahī*), is the indicator of the third and fourth feet [of the mantra], which is *māyā*. 61.

According to the Smṛti, "Oṃ tat sat—this threefold designation is recorded as belonging to Brahman," and according to the Śruti, "That is the eternal Brahman," the referent of the word *tat* is Brahman. Furthermore, that very same [Brahman] is the meaning of the syllable *ka*, based on the Śruti, "Ka is Brahman"; or else, its meaning is "He who desires" (*kāmayate*).
The suffix *ḍa* is derived from the *uṇādi* [list].

He who desires is a *kāmī*; he himself, being stainless (*nirañjana*), manifests as the state of desirelessness and is thus designated as "desire" (*kāma*). Through the contemplation of that, "desire" (*kāma*) pervades the letter *ka*.

On account of the scripture; that is, on account of the scripture stating "Kāmeśvara. Thus, "Kāmeśvara" is the final established term. However, "Savitṛ" ends in a primary suffix (pratyaya), like the usage in the Kalpasūtra: "before driving away the calves," and so forth. It is the cause of the procreation of living beings; that is to say, it is the *yoni* (womb/source). And that—

Because it is not shared by others, it is *vareṇya*, meaning most excellent and worthy of worship. By these two words, its status as the source of the universe (*jagadyonitva*) is established; and by that, the sense of "Kāmeśvarī" is obtained.
That same meaning is also conveyed by the letter *e* (ekāra), because it is triangular in shape. And thus says the Śruti:

Regarding the mantra *saviturvareṇyam*, the root *ṣūñ* means "the procreation of living beings. Starting with the statement that "Savitṛ procreates living beings," it is explained that he procreates by means of the triangle, which is the form of Śakti and the Great Vagina (*mahābhaga*);
therefore, it is said that the letter *e* alone is to be grasped, and so forth.
This seed-syllable, which is the eleventh support and consists of three corners,
is that by which the entire world— from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) down to the shell— is seen even today.

Thus it is clearly seen in the Vāmakeśvaratantra. Regarding the word "sarva" (all): the meaning of the word *deva* is "the inner ruler of all," according to the scripture, "The deity is that which dwells in the center. *Sa-urṅas*: *dhatta* means "it supports," hence *dhīḥ*. *Dadhat*: the meaning is "the support of the universe," according to the scripture, "Dhara is so called because it is supported (*dhāryate*) as consciousness (*dhī*)."

"Bharga" has a clear meaning; it culminates in the sense that Śiva is the inner controller of all and the support of all. Such is the meaning of the vowel *ī* as well. Beginning with "Bhargo devasya," the fourth syllable is contained within everything. That fourth syllable is...

It has been explained as being situated between the words; therefore, according to the Śruti, "the *ī* [belongs] to the *bhargas* of the God, the *dhīs*" (*tasmād bhargo devasya dhīty evam īkāraḥ*). Its meaning is that of the Fourth (*turya*); however, in the mantra, because even the third [letter] is the Fourth in the sequence of the Mātṛkā, it is the meaning of the letter *ī*. *Mahī* means the earth (*pṛthvī*).

Because of its magnitude and solidity—this is an illustration of the five great elements (mahābhūtas). Just as in the expression "the clay pot" (*mṛd-ghaṭaḥ*), the meaning of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in having a single case-ending is that [the pot] has undergone transformation (*pariṇata*) into the nature of that [clay]. And this very [transformation] is the [nature] of the seed of earth.

The meaning of the letter *la* is as follows: having begun the explanation of the word "mahī" (earth) with the passage "together with the oceans and mountains," etc., the entire terrestrial sphere (*bhūmaṇḍala*) is established;
for according to the scripture, it is said that "the terrestrial sphere itself is expressed by the letter *la*. Thus, [it is] the third.

The third foot of the Gāyatrī is "dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt," which means that [the Lord] impels the intellects of people like us toward an object that is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and devoid of meditation and the like. In other words, it is the generator of knowledge regarding the supreme reality (paratattva). The fourth foot is "parorajase."

"Sāvadoṃ. [This means] "beyond the *rajas*, further than the *rajas*. By the rule *soḥ śe*, the substitution of *śe* occurs. It is that which has transcended *rajas*. The meaning is either "stainless" (*nirmala*) or "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*), because since the word *rajas* denotes dust, it is possible for it to indicate the three *guṇas* by synecdoche. That is to say, it is beyond the three *guṇas*. But it is not "other" (*para*).

In this context, one should not mistake the words for being separate, because in the *Subrahmaṇyā* liturgical recitation they are used as "parorajāste pañcamaḥ pādaḥ" (the fifth foot is beyond the dust). Regarding the phrase "sāvadom," it means that the *praṇava* (Om) which both contains speech (*savat*) and is beyond speech (*avat*), is both capable of being expressed by words and incapable of being expressed by words. By words.

It cannot be understood through primary denotation (*śakti*), because the property that serves as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka-dharma*) is absent in the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). However, it can be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because [the Supreme Reality] possesses the relation of identity with that which is qualified by the denotata of words such as "Truth" (*satya*) and "Knowledge" (*jñāna*). This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "From which words turn back."

"I alone am to be known by all the Vedas," and according to such Smṛti texts as "the indicated meaning is accessible through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā)," the meaning of the Praṇava is the Supreme Reality, which consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra through the syllables A, U, and M.

This much is also the meaning of *hṛllekhā*. The meaning of the syllable *hr̥* is "heart" (*hṛdaya*). In that context, *ī* means "gone. This root is included in the group beginning with *iṭakiṭakaṭī gatau* (meaning "to go"). For this very reason, there is a scriptural statement (*śruti*) that "Hṛllekhā dwells in the temple of the heart. And thus, this is the meaning of the *Gāyatrī*.

And from the first peak (kūṭa), Kāmeśvara—who possesses the desire in the form of the wish to create the entire world—is manifested; Kāmeśvarī, who is the cause of the world, is also manifested; and Śiva, the inner controller of all and the support of all, is manifested as having transformed into the nature of the five great elements and so forth.

The Supreme Reality is that which generates non-conceptual knowledge having as its object the mere nature of the other (the Absolute), which is stainless, devoid of qualities, accessible through the Vedas by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but inaccessible through their primary power (*śakti*); it is the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. || 60, 61 ||
He states the meaning of the second and third peaks: "The three-footed [verse] is to be understood through three syllables; above that, the fourth is indicated by six syllables.
Now, in the third [peak], the pair of syllables is indicated by the three-footed [verse] and the six-syllable [phrase]. (62)
Regarding the two peaks, the remainder is to be inferred as before; such is the case for the Vidyā.
The meaning of the Gāyatrī has been explained in the Tripuropaniṣad and likewise in the Bhāgavata.

Regarding "tripadī gāyatrī," one should understand that "three-footed" (padatraya) is to be understood by means of the three syllables situated in the second *kūṭa*. "Trivarṇāḥ" refers to syllables consisting of three parts (*tryavayavakāḥ*). The compound is to be analyzed like "triguṇasacivaḥ" or "navarasarucirām" and so forth.

The referent of the word *tat* (that) is the meaning of the letter *ha*, which denotes Brahmā-Śiva; for the Śruti, beginning with "the Supreme Self is *tat*" and stating that "the syllable *ha* is the form of Śiva," finally demonstrates Śakti by means of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the word *tat*. [Likewise,] the letter *sa* is Savitṛ.

The meaning is as follows: the letter *ka* signifies the "most excellent" (*vareṇya*). The fourth letter is *ha*; that which exists above it, over the three words, is the six-syllable mantra "bhargo devasya dhī," and [the letter *ka*] conveys its meaning.
In the third *kūṭa*, there are two letters, *sa* and *ka*.

The meaning of the *gāyatrī* ending in *dhīti* is to be established by those two; in both cases, the meaning begins with "by means of the letter *la* and *hṛllekhā*, as the essence of the five great elements," etc.—thus he says, "in the pair of *kūṭas*. In this way, the four-footed *gāyatrī* is repeated three times.
The expression "the triad of verses that establishes the meaning" refers to the *Bhāgavata*. That which belongs to the Goddess (*bhagavatī*) is the *Bhāgavata*;
the meaning is that it is found therein, namely in the *Bhagavatī-purāṇa*. For the first verse of that Purāṇa is recited as consisting of three quarters, as follows:
"Let us meditate upon that primordial Vidyā, whose nature is pure consciousness;
may she impel our intellect.
For here, it is indeed the primordial Śrīvidyā alone that possesses the nature of Brahman.

That the Gāyatrī and other mantras are expounded therein, as well as that the Brahmavidyā is expounded, is clear to those who have observed the explanations of its meaning. In reality, however, it is the Hayagrīva-Brahmavidyā wherein the slaying of Vṛtra occurs.
And its commencement is with the Gāyatrī; indeed, they know that to be the Bhāgavata.

Thus, by following these characteristics, this alone is what is denoted by the term *bhāgavata*, and not [the definition] beginning with "from which the birth etc. of this [world proceeds through conjunction" (janmādy asya yato ’nvayāt) and so forth]. || 62, 63 ||

Now, he states the six meanings, beginning with the meaning of the essential nature (bhāvārtha), as taught in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Vāmā and Icchā are Brahmā and Bhāratī; Jyeṣṭhā and Jñāna are Hari and Kṣiti;
Raudrī and Kriyā are Śiva and Aparṇā—this is the triad of couples. (64)
The three peaks are to be expressed by the three *ī* sounds respectively;
that which consists of the synthesis of these three is the object of expression, whose nature is Śānta and Ambikā. (65)

The three powers—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—are constituent parts of Light (prakāśa), while Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are its constituent parts in male form. Their collective totality (samaṣṭi) is the fourth power, whose nature is Peace (śāntā). The powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action are constituent parts of Self-reflection (vimarśa).

The three powers (śakti) well-known as his wives—Bhāratī, Pṛthivī, and Rudrāṇī—are female in form; their collective totality (samaṣṭi) is the fourth power, whose essence is Ambikā. And herein, the first triad of couples constitutes, respectively, the meaning of the three seed-syllables (kūṭa) excluding the vowel *ī*.

However, the meaning of the *ī*-vowels is the fourth couple. But regarding the meaning of the Śakti [as it will be] explained below, even in each individual *kūṭa*, the meaning is three couples consisting of the six letters ending with the letter *ra*;
therefore, there is a distinction. As it has been said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

O Dear One, the meaning of the syllables is indeed the essential meaning, which is the absolute Supreme Goddess; likewise, O Beloved, the King of Mantras is always generated by the Yoginīs, the Vīras,
and the lords of Vīras through the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Thus it is said. And this has been explained by Amṛtānandayogin:
[it refers] to the yoginīs such as Māraṇī and others, and to the lords of heroes (vīrendras) such as Brahmā and others, who are the denotations of the three peak-syllables (kūṭa).

The meaning is that the King of Mantras is produced— that is, manifested— by the Couple, which is the unified form of Śiva and Śakti and is denoted by the syllable *E*, and is meditated upon by the *vīras*. In reality, however,
the three types of practitioners named Sakala and so forth, who will be described later, are designated by the term *vīra*.
Bringing about the dissolution of this "this-ness" (idamaḥ), which is its opposite,
and intent upon supreme valor, I enjoy my own Self, which removes all inauspiciousness.

Because, in the *Parāpañcāśikā* and elsewhere, the term "hero" (*vīra*) is etymologically defined specifically as referring to the practitioner (*sādhaka*), for this very reason Brahmā and the others are designated by the title "Lord of Heroes" (*vīrendra*) due to their being the most excellent among worshippers.

This is consistent. And this being so, the three Yoginīs beginning with Bhāratī, the three practitioners (sādhakas) beginning with Sakala, and the three Vīrendras beginning with Brahmā are to be represented respectively by the three *kūṭas* [of the mantra] excluding *hṛllekhā*. As for the *hṛllekhās*, however—

The meaning is the fourth couple, consisting of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, because of the statement that the syllable *hrīṃ* is composed of both. The meaning of "mantra" is that which is produced by or joined with the Yoginīs and others who constitute its denotative objects. || 64, 65 ||
Keeping this very point in mind, he says:
"Alternatively, for Speech and all [the other goddesses] beginning with Brahmā, there is a triad for each;
that which is expressed by the three peaks is Māyā, while the fourth is considered to be the couple. (66)

Alternatively, the term *vīra* is a qualifying attribute of the *yoginīs* themselves, and its gender is not fixed. For this very reason, Brahmā and the others are designated by the term *vīrendra*, which denotes the lord of heroes (*vīrapati*).
Furthermore, through the two terms *yoginī* and *vīrendra*, [the reference is made] to those who will be described later in the context of the Śākta meaning.
There is a reference to the six syllables that denote Brahmā, Bhāratī, and so forth.
By the term "the union of Śiva and Śakti," there is a reference to the Kāmakalā,
in which the conjunction of both [aspects] follows immediately thereafter.
Because it will be explained later. Thus, the meaning is that the King of Mantras is generated—that is, manifested—by these seven syllables repeated three times.

The sense is that because the mantra is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of this group of seven, it is also of that same nature, according to the principle of the ultimate reality of expansion (*prasāra-paramārtha-nyāya*). And not...

If the origin of the mantra were accepted, its beginninglessness would be destroyed; for, since everything other than the undifferentiated Brahman is admitted to be produced— on the basis of the authority of the scriptures that teach creation—
the quality of being unproduced (anāditva) cannot be intended for it, just as it is not intended for the qualified power (saviśeṣa-śakti).
However, the beginninglessness of the stream (*pravāha-anāditva*) is not untenable even if one accepts that things are produced,
because it is admitted that every effect exists in a subtle form within its cause even prior to its manifestation, by virtue of all effects possessing two forms: the gross and the subtle.

Since we, as proponents of *satkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause), accept this, statements establishing beginninglessness can be interpreted as having that very [pre-existence] as their intended meaning. However, in the first two positions, the meaning of terms such as "produced" (*janita*) is not natural. For this very reason, in the subsequent text:

The demonstration of the non-difference of the mantra from the Supreme Deity, who is the collective totality (samastirūpa) of the seven goddesses beginning with Bhāratī, is consistent, since the mantra consists of the collective totality of the phonemes that denote [her].

For us, who maintain the non-difference between the signifier and the signified, the identity of the supreme deity—who is the aggregate of all denotable meanings—is established by logic; thus, the integrity of our composition is maintained. For example:
Having realized the Goddess— who is composed of that [reality], who is gladdened by supreme bliss, whose form is vibration, and who is beautiful by nature— they worship her freely.
In the eternal Brahman, whose nature is the union of Śiva and Śakti,
which is characterized by Indraśila (the diamond-like sapphire) because it is embraced by the expansion of its own manifestation;
Because she effects the forms consisting of knowledge for the knower, she is the nature of mantra;
as the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of them, the Supreme Power is indeed Mātṛkā.

Thus [it is said]. "Consisting of that" (*tanmayīm*) means non-different from the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here to denote non-difference, as in the expressions "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) or "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*). Others, however, explain the meaning of the fourth peak (*kūṭa*) as follows:
"consisting of that" means that which is expressed by the mantra which is the aggregate of the three groups of syllables denoting the four couples.

They explain it thus; however, that is not entirely consistent with the literary context, and since there is an absence of the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of "consisting of," it should be disregarded. *Spanda* is the transformation into the nature of the thirty-six *tattvas*;
[the Goddess is] "of that form," meaning non-different from that. By this, [it is shown that] the universe, which is non-different from the Deity—

The non-differentiation of the mantra has been indicated. It is precisely the state of the undifferentiated manifold of name and form (nāmarūpa-prapañca) being ready for emergence that is designated by such terms as "vibration" (spanda), "unfolding" (unmeṣa), and "differentiation" (vyākaraṇa); nothing else whatsoever stirs.

"In the passage beginning with 'I shall manifest name-and-form (nāmarūpa), for indeed one who is not skilled cannot even move,' the conventional usage in the Tantras is generally that movement belongs only to the world of unmanifest name-and-form. Thus, one who contemplates the non-difference between the mantra, the deity, and the world..."

He prescribes that one should mutter the mantra with the words "svairam upāsata" (one should worship at will). Here, this fifth *lakāra* (the suffix -ta) has the sense of the optative (*liṅ*). Just as in the expression "mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti" (he sleeps with his mouth open), the suffix *-ktvā* in "jñātvā" (having known) is used despite the simultaneity of the actions. In this way, [the author] establishes the non-difference of the mantra from the deity through logical arguments.
