Would the designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) apply to the syllable *haṃsa* because of the presence of the letter *s*, and in its absence, would the designation "heavy" (*guru*)—by the rule "in a conjunction [the preceding vowel is] heavy"—not be established for the vowel *ā* belonging to the letter *h*? For that [designation] is indeed desired. This very point is addressed in the treatise on prosody by the *Piṅgala-sūtra*: "followed by *dhra* and so forth."

This has been explained by us in the *Candobhāskara*. Likewise, since the purpose is already fulfilled by the *Prātiśākhya* sūtra "saṃyogādi" (beginning of a conjunct), which prescribes that the first consonant of a conjunct syllable belongs to the preceding [vowel], the separate rule "anusvāraḥ" is unnecessary.

It is useless; for nowhere in either the world or the Veda is an anusvāra seen following a vowel at the end of a word, which would render it meaningful. Therefore, one must necessarily state that the subject of the separate formulation of this rule is specifically the anusvāra of the Śrīvidyā. And by that—

The *bindus* are indeed the limbs (*aṅgas*) of the *kāmakalās* themselves; as for the *nāda*, it will be a vowel (*svara*) without consonantal limbs, like the second and third vowels—this is the general direction. And this relationship of limb and possessor of limbs (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is found in the Veda in such passages as "the *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables."
Even though worldly desires (*laukikacchanda*) are the subject at hand,
they are employed for the purpose of establishing the number fifteen, sixteen, and so forth,
by counting the syllables of the primary [mantra] as non-different from them, through the intended expression of non-difference between the constituent parts (*aṅga*) and the whole (*aṅgin*).

The actual state of affairs is that the completion of the number is necessary; however, to provide an exception to that, it was stated "by way of the distinction between vowels and consonants. The meaning is that in the context of the subject at hand, one must effect a distinction between the part (aṅga) and the whole (aṅgin), and their non-distinction should not be intended. For, in the case of the Hādividyā—
Since the second and third syllables also possess consonants, there are sixty syllables.
Even if one accepts that the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the others constitute single phonemes (*ekavarṇa*), there are still thirty-nine.
However, if one accepts that the drops (*bindu*) are also single phonemes by merging them into the sounds (*nāda*), there are thirty-six.

In that regard, there are forty powers: the six seed-syllables of space (*vyomabīja*), the three *māyās*, the single causal bindu (*kāraṇabindu*), and three each of the *repha*, moon-seed, earth-seed, Krodheśa-bindu, and nāda—making twelve; and the Śrīkaṇṭhas [are] likewise. Thus is the establishment of their meaning, and so forth.
In some way, that number thirty-seven is established. Although its proponents maintain that there are fifteen vowels,
eighteen consonants, three *bindus*, and one as the aggregate of all letters— thus making thirty-seven— as it is stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:

Vidyā is that which manifests through the divisions of the vowels, consonants, the three bonds, and their collective totality; she is the essence of the thirty-six principles, yet transcends all principles, and is absolute.

Thus, even so, because number has the inherent nature of being established as distinct, the re-counting of that which has already been counted in its individual form is secondary; furthermore, it results in the fifteenth [day] becoming the sixteenth. Moreover, regarding the non-difference between the limb and the possessor of limbs...

One must consider how the inclusion of the fifteen phonemes, which are established in common worldly usage, as non-distinct entities is obtained, given that the text explicitly states "by way of distinction" (*bhedena*) for the purpose of refuting what is so established. Even though...
In cases such as *bhedapadasya saṃbhedaḥ* ("the confluence of the word *bheda*"), since the term *saṃbheda* is well-known in the sense of "conjunction" (*saṃgama*),

it is also easy to explain it here as meaning "by the meeting of all vowels and consonants. Nevertheless, there is a strain on the usage of the word *bheda*, because it is not preceded by the prefix *sam*.

And [it possesses] the capacity to express such a meaning. Furthermore, for instance, by the statement "that [vowel] is pervaded by fifteen phonemes," the fact of having fifteen syllables is stated in general, and then, in order to establish that [fact]:

In the subsequent text, there is a specific statement using the terms "with five" and likewise "with six," as well as a general statement regarding the possession of thirty-seven syllables through the distinction between vowels and consonants,
beginning with the phrase "divided into thirty-seven parts."

It is undisputed that, having made this promise, the author establishes it by analyzing it through the subsequent text beginning with "by means of the seed-syllables of space situated in the Vidyā-mantra" and ending with "the awakening of the three Nāndīs. And therein, according to the aforementioned method—
Even by providing forty [syllables], the contradiction between the introduction and the conclusion remains difficult to resolve.
Furthermore,
it is said that Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva are denoted by three *bindus*.
Śānti, Śakti, and Śambhu are the awakeners of the triad of Nādas.
Thus, within a single verse, by describing the meaning of both the three *bindus* and the three *nādas*, there is a clear partiality at work:
namely, that while the three *bindus* are mentioned for the sake of completing the number thirty-seven, the three *nādas* are omitted. By this [it is shown] in the case of the *Kādī-vidyā*:

In order to establish the number thirty-seven, the ancients have rejected the difficulty of counting the second and third syllables as each having a dual nature due to their being *saṃdhyakṣaras* (diphthongs);
for such an approach would lead to the same consequence even in the case of the *hṛllekhās*, thereby resulting in a contradiction of the present subject matter.
Therefore, the state of thirty-seven [principles] arises precisely through the union of the three *nādas*. This is clearly stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"By means of the letters produced from the three *hṛllekhas*, which are equal in number to the lunar days (fifteen)," since one counts five letters for each *hṛllekha* repeatedly.

Therefore, let those of impartial intellect understand that in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, in the section concerning the meaning of the tradition (*saṃpradāyārtha-prakaraṇa*), everything beginning with the letter *ka* is inherently [contained] within the *Kādividyā* alone.
This is the essential point here: [the letters] denote and indicate their respective objects through those very syllables.
By pointing to the constituent objects (*padārtha*) with the eleventh vowel, their non-difference from Brahman, who transcends the categories (*tattva*), is enjoined.

Likewise, because [the universe] consists of the collection of objects denoted by the aggregate of syllables that are the components of the Vidyā, it is also enjoined that the universe is non-different from the Vidyā. For, in the sense of the verbal root...

There is one cognition whose subject (uddeśya) is both knowledge (*vidyā*) and the world (*jagat*), whose qualificand (vidheya) is the non-difference between Śiva and Śakti as indicated by the fact of being produced from Śiva and Śakti;
and [another] whose qualificand is the non-difference from the universe, as indicated by the fact of being produced from that which produces the universe.

And there is one [mantra] that enumerates the Vidyās; however, in this context, the single mantra that enumerates the Vidyās is that which makes known the fact of being composed of the single syllable that is the specific designator for every object included within the universe, and which has non-difference from the universe as its predicate.
And there is another cognition which has the differentiation of knowledge as its object of prescription with the universe as its intended object; such is the distinction. || 80 ||
Intending this very point, he says:

"Because there is no difference between the produced and the producer, the expressed is also [non-different] from the expresser; thus, the distinction between the world and Brahman, as well as within the world itself, is for the sake of the traditional teaching. (81)
In the phrase "of the world in Brahman," the word "non-difference" (abheda) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The meaning of "saṃpradāya" (tradition) is that which is given according to the established limits transmitted through the proper succession of gurus and disciples. || 81 ||
Now he states the meaning of the *nigarbha*:

"The partless state in Paramaśiva, the non-difference from Him on the part of one's own supreme teacher, and through His compassion, the non-difference from Him within oneself—this is the *nigarbha* meaning. (82)

Supreme Śiva is Brahman, as described in its essential nature at the conclusion of the determination of the Kāmakalā; therein, "partlessness" (niṣkalatā) means the absence of all other entities, because everything else is a source of suffering, according to the Vedic scripture: "From duality, indeed, fear arises. Thus it is said.
This is the meaning of the first peak (kūṭa). By that [realization], there is non-difference between Brahmā and one's own supreme teacher, the venerable feet of the Guru;
for, through the firmness of the contemplation of their non-difference from Brahmā, that non-difference is established.
This is the meaning of the second peak (kūṭa). From that compassion,

by the power of a glance mixed with the guru’s great mercy— which arises from the favor produced by very firm service preceded by one's own performed and unswerving devotion— even toward the practitioner themselves...

The non-difference from Brahman is established; this is the meaning of the third peak (kūṭa). Because it effects one's own entry into the womb of Śiva by means of the Guru, the object of this knowledge is the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self, which is denoted by the term "nigama-artha" (the meaning of the Vedic tradition). || 82 ||
Now, the identity of the Supreme Deity, the Vidyā, the King of Wheels (cakrarāja),

the venerable Guru, and one's own self is called the *kaulikārtha* (the Kaula meaning), because all these are of the same nature through their non-difference from Brahman, and because a group consisting of members of the same nature is denoted by the term *kula*.

According to Amara’s statement, "a *kula* or *yūtha* consists of those of the same class (*sajātīya*)," this non-difference of the five is intended to be established by virtue of their possessing common attributes. And that common attribute is [the Goddess] who takes the form of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, and the zodiac signs.
I bow to the Goddess who consists of mantra, whose form is the seat of the Mātṛkās.

Thus concludes the section titled "The Nature of Being Composed of the Sixfold Group Beginning with Gaṇeśa," as stated in the *Tantrarāja*. Therein, he first establishes the nature of Gaṇeśa within the Supreme Deity:
"The Mother [is the source] of the rays that are her own, consisting of incomparable splendor."
She is called Gaṇeśī because she is the sovereign of the presiding deities of the obstructions. || 83 ||
The deities of the veil are the very rays of the Brahman, whose nature is infinite splendor as established by such scriptural passages as "There the sun does not shine.
These number one hundred and eleven; according to different tantras, there are others as well.
She has been thus established. Because she is the sovereign (Īśī) over such a host of deities (Gaṇa), the Mother is called Gaṇeśī.

The Mother is said to have the form of the planets because she is composed of the ninefold union of the three—desire and the rest—endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), and presided over by Fire, the Moon, and the Sun. 84.

The Mother is the unified totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three powers—will, knowledge, and action. As it is said in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "Will is in the region of the head, then knowledge is situated below that, and action is indeed located in her feet. [This refers to] that which is distinguished by its qualities.

The qualities are designated as being merely the constituent parts of the variegated Brahman (*śabalabrahman*). In the present context, because the *grahas* such as the Sun and others are nine in number, they possess exactly nine constituent parts.
The state of being a planet (grahatva) is intended [to be understood here]. In this very same way, it should be understood regarding the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) and so forth as well. || 84 ||

The Mother, whose form is that of the stars, is born from the ten sense organs, the fourfold internal organ, the ten objects of the senses, and the principles of primordial nature, the individual soul, and the qualities (guṇas). 85.

The five organs of knowledge, beginning with the ear; the five organs of action, beginning with speech—these are the ten organs. The fourfold internal organ consists of the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta). And there are the ten objects: sound and the rest, as well as speech and the rest.

*Prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*; *puruṣa* is the individual self; and the *guṇatattva* is the root of pleasure, pain, and delusion, consisting of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three *guṇas*, such as *sattva*.
Thus, because she consists of twenty-seven principles, the Mother is of the nature of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). || 85 ||

By the six Ākinīs, beginning with the syllables *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-ha*, which are encircled by the letters preceded by *a-ka-ḍa-ba-va-ha* in numbers equal to the kings (16), suns (12), directions (10), seasons (6), oceans (4), and twice (2).
With her body thus formed, she is called a Yoginī. || 86 ||
The lords of men are sixteen kings; the suns are twelve; the directions are ten, since the two directions of above and below are included within the eight cardinal points;
and the oceans are four, as in the expression "having the four oceans as her breasts" and so forth.
This is because the number [of vowels] is well-known as being like that of the oceans.
The numbers sixteen and so forth are correlated with the letters beginning with *a* according to their respective order.
The sixteen vowels beginning with *a* are indicative of the sixteen deities beginning with Amṛtā.
The twelve syllables from *ka* to *ṭha* are indicative of Kālarātri and the others;

the ten from *ḍa* to *pha* are indicative of Ḍāmari and the others; the six from *ba* to *la* are indicative of Bandhinī and the others; and the four from *va* to *sa* [are indicative of the remaining goddesses].
Of Varadā and the others: the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* are indicative of Haṃsavatī and Kṣamāvatī.

Those Ākinīs whose initial constituent is the group of six letters beginning with *ḍa* are Ḍākinī and the rest. Thus, Ḍākinī is surrounded by Amṛtā and the others, and [Rākinī] is surrounded by Kālarātri and the others.
By the manner [of the goddess] Rākinī, through the six [deities] who are the presiding lords of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow, there are petals in the respective wheels—
the Viśuddha, Anāhata, Maṇipūra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Mūlādhāra, and Ājñā—
equal in number to the powers (śakti) of the respective surrounding retinues of those deities.

The meaning is that she is called a *yoginī* because her body is composed of the Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī who are seated upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of those [lotuses] surrounded by as many goddesses as have been mentioned. Even though...

"Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents (dhātus)"— this is the well-known proclamation of physicians regarding the seven constituents; likewise, their presiding deity, known by the name Yākinī,
resides in the thousand-petaled lotus, whose petals are variegated by the presence of the entire host of powers beginning with Amṛtā.

"It abides" is well-known in the Tantras; furthermore, her placement (*nyāsa*) is seen even in some Tantras within the *ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*. Nevertheless, because the *Yoginīhṛdaya* prescribes the placement of only six [powers], there is no power distinct from the powers beginning with Amṛtā that exists in the form of an enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).
Because there is no distinction between this group of six as a collective whole and the subject (mātṛ) who consists of non-existence, there are only six Yoginīs. As it has been said:
"In the Viśuddhi, the Heart, the Navel, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Mūla."

O Queen of the Gods, the lords of the elements should be placed within the command (ājñā), and the deities beginning with *ḍa* should be properly meditated upon as endowed with nectar and other [substances].
Thus [ends the verse]. 86.

Through the five [elements] beginning with Nāga and Kūrma, through the five [winds] beginning with Prāṇa and Apāna, and through the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), she is of the nature of an aggregate.

By the two words "first" (*ādi*) and so forth, there is an inclusion of Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya, as well as Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna. Thus, because she consists of twelve aspects, the Mother of the World has the form of a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*). Of the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*)...

Since they possess a number equal to that of Gaṇeśa and the others, their nature is effectively stated by the very mention of those [deities]; therefore, there is no further separate effort required here. || 87 ||

Now, he establishes that the Vidyā possesses the form of Gaṇeśa and others: "The Vidyā also has the form of Gaṇeśa, for it is composed of the third [seed-syllable] Kāma and the Vāgbhava, consisting of sixteen syllables beginning with 'A-Ka-THa', and it is also joined with the groups of speech beginning with Parā."
The third peak-syllable (kūṭa), consisting of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, is the Śakti-peak.
The second, the Kāmarāja-peak, consists of the letters from *ka* to *ta*.
The first, the Vāgbhava-peak, is composed of the letters from *tha* to *sa*.
This [Śrīvidyā] consists of the fourfold speech beginning with *parā*, distinguished by its individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) aspects.
Therefore, because she is the sovereign of the multitude of sounds, Śrīvidyā is also the form of Gaṇeśa. The meter here is Vaitālīya;
her status as a planet is established here through the three *bindus*, the three *nādas*, and the other three *kūṭas*.
And the state of being a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) belongs to the ten aspects because they are not distinct from their phonemes. || 89 ||

"Released from *bindu* and *nāda*" means that each *kūṭa* consists of one *bindu*, one *nāda*, and one [syllable]; thus, for every *kūṭa*, there are three. As it has been said: "The nature of the planets resides in the *bīja*, *bindu*, and *dhvani* within the three *kūṭas*. This refers to the *dvandva* compound *bindavaśca dhvanayaśca*.

From the *tatpuruṣa* compound "bindu-dhvani" [meaning] "the sounds of the drops of the seeds," and by that word "bīja-bindu-dhvanīnām" (of the seeds, drops, and sounds), six are counted. The remainder [of the meaning] is that there is a merging of those six within the three peaks—that is, in the three [peaks] distinct from them. Alternatively, the meaning of the genitive case is "belonging to" (*saṃbandhitva*).

The construction is as follows: when those six are combined and calculated among the *kūṭas*, the science consisting of the planets (*grahātmikā vidyā*) arises. Those who, having explained [the term] as "tripadadvandva," establish the planetary nature by means of the mere seed-syllable (*bīja*) accompanied by the separation of its constituent parts.

For them, the other parts [of the Vidyā] would be rendered useless; furthermore, since it is stated that the complete Vidyā itself consists of Gaṇeśa, the Nakṣatras, and so forth, there would be an inconsistency in establishing that only a single part of the Vidyā constitutes a *graha* in some instances, while the whole constitutes one in others.

And furthermore, we shall explain immediately below how even for a *yoginī* and others, there is no occurrence of being a mere partial form (*ekadeśarūpatā*). Moreover, since that which is devoid of the *bindu* lacks the status of being a seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is also not appropriate to refer to it by the term "seed-syllable. Otherwise, how could [the text] say: "pure [and] joined with the *bindu*"?
Thus, within the section on the *śuddhamātṛkā-nyāsa*— which is one of the ten types of *mātṛkā-nyāsa* beginning with these—
it is stated that when the *bindu* (the nasal dot) is omitted, the mere syllables would acquire the status of seed-syllables (*bīja*). Consequently,
even though this would result in redundancy when performing the *nyāsa* with the *bindu*, the pure *nyāsa* (*śuddha-nyāsa*) must be performed precisely with the *bindu*.
The statement of the traditionalists (sāṃpradāyika) is thus consistent; this is the general direction.

In the section on the meaning of the tradition (saṃpradāyārtha-prakaraṇa), thirty-seven phonemes were mentioned. Among those, when ten of the Śrīkaṇṭhas are counted together with their respective consonants, they constitute the number ten.

When [the letters] are excluded, twenty-seven remain; by this, its nature as the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) is established, as he says: "And the state of being a lunar mansion... As it has been stated:
"By means of the syllables produced from the three *hṛllekhās*, which are equal in number to the lunar days (*tithi*)."
This [goddess], whose form is that of the lunar mansions, consists of twelve other syllables.
Thus [ends the verse]. || 89 ||
Through union with the three *hṛllekhās* and the other *kūṭas*, this [Yoginī], though composed of many parts, becomes unified with the first syllables of those three. (90)

This Vidyā is called Yoginī because of its union with six elements: the three *hṛllekhās* and the three *kūṭas* (syllabic peaks) devoid of them. When the three *hṛllekhās* are counted together with the preceding letters, the *lakāras*:

Because it possesses twelve constituent parts, it also takes the form of a *rāśi* (an aggregate). And it has been said: "The state of being a *Yoginī* belongs to the Vidyā through the six Śākta syllables beginning with Śakti which are included within the Vidyā; and its state of being a *rāśi* [is established] by those same syllables excluding the last one."

Thus: by those three Śākta [mantras], which consist of four, five, and three syllables respectively, and which are the primordial portions of Śakti included within the Vidyā; the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), or else in the sense of a connection consisting of association (*sāhitya*). [They are] with the three.

"Accompanied by the Śaktis" means that they have attained the number six. Some, however, maintain that the word *śākta* refers to the three *la*-letters, and that the phrase "by those very [letters] with Śakti and so forth" is an adjective for them;
this is intended to indicate their association with the Śaktis, and thereby the completion of the number six. And thus...

They explain [the passage] as meaning "by the three *la*-sounds and the three *la*-shames. In their view, since only a single part of the Vidyā possesses the form of a Yoginī, the statement that "the Yoginī-nature belongs to the Vidyā" results in a violation of natural consistency (*svārasyabhaṅga*), because it would necessitate a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "Vidyā" to a mere portion of the Vidyā.

But this must be considered: since it is quite clear that the three *lakāra*s beginning with *śa* are Śākta, and the three *sakāra*s [beginning with *ha*] are likewise, even though the preference for the *Hādividyā* (the *vidyā* beginning with *ha*) is more appropriate here, why have those who favor that [other] position explained the word "power" (*śakti*) as having the meaning of the letter *la*? [This is done] by means of the [consonants] excluding the last one.

The meaning is that the separate counting of these final *māyās* must be avoided; the implication is that they should be combined by merging them with the adjacent *lakāras*. For those, however, who explain this according to the literal reading, the natural elegance (*svārasya*) of the term "of the Vidyā" would be lost.

Alternatively, since the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) consist of two and a quarter constellations (*nakṣatra*), the fact that the Full Vidyā constitutes a sign is established by the very statement that it is a constellation; however, the expression "excluding the last" is used to highlight the distinction that the status of being a sign exists even in a single part [of the constellation]. || 90 ||
Thus, although it has been established that the state of being a group of six (ṣaṭkatva) within the Vidyā serves as a proof for its non-difference from the Goddess,
nevertheless— by the very force of the scriptural statement— that the Vidyā possesses an internal form identical to the Goddess is also proven,
just as in the case of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; therefore, the state of being a group of six is established precisely through this non-difference as the logical reason.
He establishes this:

because the Vidyā is non-different from the Goddess due to being a different form of her, she possesses the nature of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, the zodiac signs, and the sacred seats (pīṭhas). 91.
Now, he describes the nature of Gaṇeśa and others within the Cakrarāja:
"Because of its construction with lines, petals, and angles, it possesses the nature of Gaṇeśa;
and because of the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana, it also possesses the nature of the planets. (92)

There are three square lines and three circular lines. There are twenty-four petals and forty-five corners. Regarding the word "trailokya" (the three worlds), the phrase "ending with [the state] consisting of all-bliss" (*sarvānandamaya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By means of the three lines composed of *A*, *Ka*, and *Tha* situated within the central triangle, one attains the state of Gaṇeśa.
In that case, there would be the fault of inconsistency (vairūpya) due to its occurrence in only one part of the "wheel of speakers" (vadatāṃ cakra). || 92 ||
By dividing the calculation of the three meters, the three earths, and the twelve months,
and adding seven other wheels, he established the form of the lunar mansions.
There are three circles for the two lotuses: two for the pericarp-circles and one outer circle.

There are three earths, which are the three lines of the subterranean chamber (*bhūgṛha*). There are fourteen corners, which are the fourteen *manu*-angles. By "the others" is meant those [mantras] other than the Trailokyamohana and the Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka.
Some say that there are three circles followed by ten spokes on the outside. || 93 ||
The two wheels of maintenance and withdrawal, the two lotuses, and the two circular earth-houses—through the union of these six, the Śrīcakra takes the form of the Yoginī. (94)

The points, the triangle, and the eight-sided figure constitute the wheel of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti-cakra*); the two ten-sided figures and the fourteen-sided figure constitute the wheel of maintenance (*sthiti-cakra*); and the remainder constitutes the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-cakra*).
This threefold nature is clearly stated in the *Cakrasaṃketaka*. Regarding the lotuses, there are those with eight petals and sixteen petals.

One square is for the earth-chamber (bhūgṛha) and one is for the [central] space; however, for those who claim that the eight corners represent the forms of the Yoginīs beginning with Brahmayā, there is extreme inconsistency. || 94 ||
Five, four, power (fire), the drop, the circle, and the orb of the earth—
by the combination of these twelve elements, the wheel possesses the nature of the zodiacal signs.
Triangles with their apexes facing oneself are called *śaktis*; there are five of them. Triangles with their apexes turned away are *anala*s; there are four of them. As it has been said:
"The arising of the *cakra* results from the conjunction of the five *śakti*s and the four *anala*s. [The *vṛtta*...]
It is encased within two lotuses. As for those who say there are nine triangles, two lotuses, and one earth-house (bhūgṛha), their fault is the omission of the *bindu*. || 95 ||
Since the non-difference [of the wheel] is established by the fact that the wheel is produced from the syllables of the Vidyā, he confirms its sixfold nature by means of that reason:
"The wheel possesses non-difference from those [syllables], because it is generated by the very syllables of the Vidyā."
And because she is a different form of the Goddess, she is joined with that aforementioned nature. || 96 ||

Although in the *Mūlatantra* the non-difference of the Vidyā within the wheel is stated only as being indicated by its being produced from those syllables, and not as being indicated by its having six forms, nevertheless, she is thus the form of the wheel, whose nature is the manifestation of the universe.
By the expression "Maheśvarī," the sixfold nature is indicated; such is the tradition. || 96 ||

When these five, beginning with Gaṇeśa, are combined, fifty-five [deities] result, because Gaṇeśa is counted as only one type; for even though there are five, seven, or nine [forms] at the lines, petals, and angles, they are conventionally designated as "one Gaṇeśa. As for the seats (pīṭhas), although...
Although there are fifty-one [sites] beginning with Kāmarūpa and ending with Chāyāchatra,
they are counted again as fifty-five by way of emphasizing the predominance of O,

JĀ, PŪ, and KĀ; thus, it is with the intention that their status as *pīṭhas* (sacred seats) is established precisely because they constitute a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of these five, that this is stated in the Tantras.
Thinking that the intention of the Tantra is not to state the nature of the *pīṭhas* as something separate [from the letters], he says:
"As many as fifty [letters] are declared to be the Mothers, joined together as one;
furthermore, the *pīṭhas* are counted as four: O, JĀ, PŪ, and KĀ. (97)
By combining the numbers of the Gaṇas, Planets, Months, Oceans, Stars, Seasons, and Suns, fifty-five sacred seats (pīṭhas) are to be known among these. 98.

The term *yāvanmātṛkam* is an avyayībhāva compound; it means that there are as many sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) as there are letters of the alphabet. [These are]: O, the sacred seat of Oḍḍiyāṇa; JĀ, the sacred seat of Jālandhara; PŪ, the sacred seat of Pūrṇagiri; KĀ, the sacred seat of Kāmarūpa. This is a case of referring to a whole by mentioning a part of its name.

Likewise, according to tradition: for the asterisms (*nakṣatra*), yoginīs, and zodiac signs (*rāśi*) beginning with *bhā*, the moon (*śaśin*) is one; the treasures (*nidhi*) are nine; and the stars (*tārā*) are twenty-seven. Even in the reading *sāra*, the letter *sa* is a convention (*saṃketika*) for the number seven, while the letter *ra* represents the number two among numerical digits.
Since it is stated that "the movement is from left to right," the aforementioned number is established by what has been said. This has been stated in Vararuci’s Paribhāṣā:
"The *pāda*s are five; those beginning with *ya* are eight; those beginning with *ka* are eight; and those beginning with *a* are nine."
This is the number of distinct syllables; the number of the bindus arises from their combination.
Thus: the seasons are six; the suns are twelve. || 97, 98 ||
Now, he establishes that the Wheel-King (*cakrarāja*) is produced from the syllables of the *vidyā* by means of two verses:
"From the third *ka* and the vowel *ī*, the bindu was born in the subsequent wheel."
The triad of wheels beyond that is formed by the *hṛllekhās* and the two *ha*-letters.
By the letter *e*, that [central] circle is formed; by the two *sa*s, the squares;
and by the *la*s, the [outer] squares—thus is the generation of the wheel from the syllables of the Vidyā. (100)
O Goddess, the supreme seat of Sadāśiva consists of the Great Bindu and is joined with the threefold Ādana in the form of will, knowledge, and action.
From this vowel *ī*, these three powers— will and the others— are manifested (*rupyante*) or produced; and that [vowel], conjoined with the triad of *ka*s (the *mādana* letters),
produces the throne of Sadāśiva consisting of the Great Bindu, namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara.

The feet [are the letters], and the plank is composed of Sadāśiva; the meaning is that such is the wheel consisting of universal bliss (*sarvānandamaya*). Alternatively, it is a *dvandva* compound: "those which are of the nature of will, knowledge, and action" (*icchājñānakriyārūpāḥ*) and "the three intoxicants" (*mādanāḥ*); by the word "three," the vowel *ī* is indicated because it consists of the three *bindus*.
The *brāhma* [portion]. The remainder is as before. This very point he states: "And that [mandala], consisting of nine wombs (*yoni*), is born from three *lajjās*;
likewise, it is formed by the letters numbering fifteen, which arise from the three *hṛllekhās*."
O Dear One, that which is born from the three drops consists of nine wombs.
He says "tadagrima" and so forth because of this statement:
the triad of wheels of persistence (sthiticakra), known as the "All-Protector," the "Accomplisher of All Aims," and the "Bestower of All Good Fortune," is fashioned by three powers and three fires.
It is produced by two *ha*-letters and the eleventh vowel. As it has been said:
"The wheel, joined with the three mandalas, consists of the nature of power (*śakti*) and fire;
[it is formed] by the three space-seeds (*vyomabīja*) alone..."
Thus: "The two decagons and the octagon" refers to the three mandalas; and "the three in the sky-seed" (*vyomabīja*)—this is the analysis [of the compound].

By the word "three," the letter *e* is indicated because it consists of three corners. Alternatively, having analyzed it as "the sky and the seed" (*vyoma ca bījam ca*), or "the three which are the sky-seeds" (*vyomabījāni eva trayam*), is another analysis.

The letter *E* is the seed-syllable (*bījapada*), because it serves as the seed for everything from the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) up to the shell of the universe (*kaṭāha*), and because of its application in the statement: "The eleventh support, which is the seed, consists of three corners. However, in the case of the *Hādi* system (where *Ha* is the first), there is no difficulty whatsoever here. This is what he says:
By the passage beginning with *tatpara* and ending with *ceti*, [it is explained].
Regarding the phrase *tatparacakre*: the meaning is "in the wheel that agitates all and fulfills all desires. And it has been said:
"The two lotuses by the Śākta-s"—that is, by the two *sakāra*s. *Akṣīṇi me*—my eyes...

This is why the plural number is used; for it is logical that there should be an equality of number between the produced and the producer whenever such a possibility exists. It is precisely for this reason that the qualification "joined with three dots" (bindutrayayutaiḥ) in the aforementioned verse regarding the "three hṛllekhās" is meaningful, given that there are fifteen syllables [in total].

When the triad of *bindu* and *nāda* is merged with the three *ī* vowels, in each *hṛllekhā* there arise precisely these three: the letter *ha*, the letter *ra*, and the vowel *ī*. Since the two wheels consisting of nine *yoni*s are produced by that group of nine syllables—namely, that triad—the word *bindu* [is used].

This is because [the text] refers to the entire collection beginning with *bindu* and ending with *unmanī*. However, if it were explained as being merely intended to proclaim its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), its purposelessness would be evident.
The squares constitute the *trailokyamohana-cakra*; in both instances, the plural number is used to denote a triad. (99, 100)
One's own guru is non-different from this triad due to the firmness of the contemplation of that non-duality;
through him, one consists of Gaṇeśa and the others, and by his grace, one becomes of that very nature oneself. (101)
He is non-different from this triad of the deities, the vidyās, and the cakras;
therefore, the venerable Guru possesses the sixfold form beginning with Gaṇeśa. By his grace, the practitioner himself [becomes so], as it has been said:
Just as the body of the Goddess has been described, so too is the body of the Guru;
and by his grace, even the disciple shines forth, being of that very same nature.
Thus: the meaning is that the bodies of these two possess exactly those very limbs and those very forms which exist in the body of the Goddess. || 101 ||

Now, one might object: how can the fivefold non-difference, which is intended to signify that [the letters] have Gaṇeśa and the others as their essence, be logically established, given that the word *gaṇa* (group) denotes a collection and thus depends upon the members of that collection— the deities, syllables, and lines— which are distinct?

Because that difference is necessary; for even though properties such as "being a lunar mansion" (nakṣatra) are subsumed under mere number, difference is accepted by those who acknowledge numbers because those possessing the numbers serve as substrata for contradictory attributes.

If it is argued that because [the individuals] are distinct from one another, no single property can have non-difference as its pervader, and thus how can non-difference— which is indicated by that [property]— be established as the probandum, do not say so; for by the very force of the statement,
the non-difference of the members of the collection and of those possessing number is established.

For it has been extensively established by the followers of the Upaniṣads— in cases such as the delusion regarding the moon's small size and elsewhere— that a word whose intended meaning has been determined through methods such as *upakrama* (initial context) possesses greater force than all other means of valid cognition, including perception. Furthermore, [the property] of being of the same class as its own substratum...

The state of being merely a number whose nature consists of its own selfhood—conjoined with the absence of any number that is either resident in it, distinct from it, or pervading it—is also a proof of non-difference, as there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
The word "self" (*sva*) refers here to numbers such as nine and so forth. By this, [the category of] knowledge (*vidyā*)...
"Because they are the substrata of the number nine, they are non-different from the nature of the deity, just like the nature of the deity"—
such are the various individual syllogisms. For this very reason, because it is the substratum of the number one alone, [the ether]—
The non-difference of Time, Space, and the Lord is accepted by the author of the *Dīdhiti*.

Furthermore, this inference, when accompanied by scripture (*āgama*), is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of producing firmness in the validity of the object; therefore, it is not...
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the non-difference between potness, clothness, and so forth.
Having all this in mind, he concludes:
"In this way, the knower, knowledge, the wheel, one's own guru, and oneself [are one]."
The absence of division even among these five is the Kaulika meaning of the mantra. || 102 ||

Now he states the meaning of all the secrets as it follows in sequence: "The Kulīnā Kuṇḍalinī, whose body is non-different from the fifty phonemes, which are filled with twelve, sixteen, and ten digits of the sun, moon, and fire. (103)

The slender one, shining like lightning, having pierced the triad of circles of fire, sun, and moon located at the root, heart, and command centers from the triangle of the *mūlādhāra* lotus, [ascends]. 104.
The twelve digits of the Sun, beginning with *Tapinī*,

are joined respectively with the twelve letters from *ka* to *bha* in direct order (*ānulomyena*), and with the twelve letters from *bha* to *ka* in reverse order (*prātilomyena*). The sixteen digits of the Moon begin with *Amṛtā*.

She is joined with the sixteen vowels. The ten digits (kalās) of Agni, beginning with Dhūmra and Arcis, are joined with the ten consonants beginning with *ya*. Thus, the Kulakuṇḍalinī, subtler than a lotus fiber, is non-different from these fifty syllables.

Resembling the tip of a lightning bolt, she is seated facing downward in the form of three and a half coils above the *śṛṅgāṭa*— the triangle situated within the pericarp of the lotus located at the *mūlādhāra*— according to the method of yoga.
It is raised upward by yogins;
it pierces the circles of fire, sun, and moon located within the *mūlādhāra*, *anāhata*, and *ājñā* cakras. (103, 104)
In the sky, having united with Akula in the midst of the lunar orb of consciousness, she causes a flood of nectar to flow forth, born from the contact of both their bodies. (105)
Having herself become intoxicated by the power of drinking that [liquor], she returns again by that very same path and sleeps happily in her own place. || 106 ||
The "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta) is above the forehead, ending at the upper part of the skull;
the region two finger-breadths above the head is proclaimed as the supreme ether (paraṃ vyoma).

Having united with the Akula-kuṇḍalinī situated in the center of the lunar orb of consciousness— which exists in the void characterized as described above and takes the form of the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus facing downwards— one causes a flood of nectar to flow from that [union].

The maṇḍalas of the Ḍākinīs and others flood [the body], and having themselves become intoxicated by drinking that, they turn back again by way of the suṣumnā and sleep happily in their own place. All of this is to be understood through the experience of yogins.

However, for those who possess only a knowledge of the boundaries of the Yoga scriptures, this [subject], which falls within the scope of indirect knowledge, must be understood by discerning it from the mouth of the Guru alone; therefore, it is not analyzed here. || 105, 106 ||
This Mother of the World is manifest knowledge itself; she is not distinct from it.
Her non-difference from this [knowledge] is the secret meaning of Śrīvidyā. (107)
The meaning is that the non-difference between such a Mother Kuṇḍalinī, who is Vidyā, and oneself is a secret matter, an unrevealed significance. || 107 ||
Now, [meditate] upon the Great Reality (mahātattva),
which is unapproachable by the organs of speech, transcending all principles, greater than the great, subtler than the subtle,
situated even above the sky, and non-different from the universe in the bliss of consciousness. || 108 ||
One's own self should be joined to the supreme Brahman for the sake of attaining non-difference from it;
this is the meaning of the great reality of Śrīvidyā as taught by Śiva. (109)

In that which is beyond speech— that is, in that which lacks the delimitor of verbal denotability (*śabda-śakyatāvacchedaka*)— and beyond the senses, such as the sixfold perception beginning with olfactory perception (*prāṇaja*),

from which words turn back without reaching it along with the mind, according to such scriptural passages as "It is without sound, without touch, without form," and so forth; and not [in that which is otherwise].

In every respect, it follows that what is not an object of knowledge would be unreal, because it is understood through words by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and because it is an object of verbal perception. [He is] beyond the principles (*tattva*), having transcended the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth; [he is] greater than the great.
It is more vast; it is unsurpassed, subtler than the subtle.

Its greatness is figuratively attributed because it is the generator of space and other elements, and its minuteness is likewise so attributed because it is not an object of gross perception; yet it is not a specific dimension.

Because that [grossness] is absent therein; for this very reason, even the Śruti passage, "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great," is consistent without contradiction. It refers to that which abides beyond the ether characterized as described above, indicated by a specific location imagined for the purpose of meditation, and which is non-different from the universe.
Because it is transformative; in consciousness, which is self-luminous; in bliss, whose nature is happiness;

in the Supreme Brahman, one's own Self is to be fixed. For the sake of attaining non-difference from That—which has remained largely unattained due to the power of one's own ignorance—one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself.
According to the scripture, because this is the root of all principles (tattvas), it is called the "Great Principle" (mahātattva).
Now, he states the meaning of the name and the meaning of the form of the sound:

"This is the meaning of each respective phoneme; this is the essential nature of each respective phoneme"—such is the meaning of the name and the meaning of the form of the sound of the Śrīvidyā. || 110 ||

By the term "those respective phonemes" (*tattad-varṇa*), the fifty-eight phonemes beginning with *ka*, or thirty-seven phonemes, or fifteen phonemes are understood; and all of these, by virtue of being denotative of Brahman, are like [the verse] "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," and so forth.

Since the coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has been established, the meaning of the sentence is obtained by completing the ellipsis with "it exists" (*asti*), based on Kātyāyana’s statement that "the present-tense [suffix] ending in the third person (*bhavantīparaḥ prathamapuruṣaḥ*) is understood even when not explicitly employed," where the phrase "ending in the present tense" (*bhavantīparaḥ*) is explained as "ending in the *laṭ* suffix."

It is to be described as follows: this being so, the meaning of the name becomes threefold—namely, consisting of fifty-eight names, thirty-seven names, and fifteen names; and in all three of these positions, [it refers to] any one of the letters beginning with 'ka'.

Because it expresses Brahman. As for the avoidance of the redundancy of other repeated syllables such as *a*, *ka*, and so forth, [it is explained] in the Viśvaprakāśa lexicon according to the rule: "The letter *a* [is used] in reference to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, tortoise, limb, and battle," and so on.
Since it has been stated that syllables can denote multiple meanings,

the explanation of the meaning should be carried out by following their respective fitness (*yogyatā*). Furthermore, according to the maxim that "wholesome advice should be spoken even a hundred times," repetition is not a fault in such instances.
And thus, because all syllables function as denoters of their respective meanings either by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or because the elision of the *s* is necessarily required for each syllable,
or because only the nominal stems remain, [the term] is well-known among those who practice meditation.

Why? Because it is taught as being the very essence of the supreme reality.
