The usage is indeed "what is called *nāman* and *ākhyāta*"; nevertheless, because of Yāska’s usage that "nouns (*nāman*) are primarily [denotative of] substances," it is possible for the word *nāman* itself to denote a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in the list of indeclinables (*avyayagaṇa*) where it says "the noun (*nāma*)."
This is because the *Kośa* states: "The term *kutsana* [denotes] manifesting, imagining, anger, and approaching.
Here, *āma* means unripe; its opposite is *nāma*. In this case, the compound is formed with the particle *na*, not with the negative particle *nañ*.
Consequently, there is no occurrence of the rule "the elision of the *n* of *nañ*" (*nalopo nañaḥ*), as is the case in words such as *nāstika*. This refers to the state of being fully ripened.
The meaning is that there is an absence of lack of aesthetic power (*virasatva*).

Regarding the statement "this [cognition] has the very nature of those respective phonemes," there too, as before, there are three possible positions. Now, one might object: "Having the nature of the letter *ka* and so forth means being non-different from the word in name; and thus, it is not that."
The meaning of the letter *ka* is fire (*h*), because there is no capacity [in the word] for its own phonetic form;

for instance, in such expressions as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the word "jar" does not connect with the act of bringing. For this very reason, even the position that the word and its meaning are non-different is not tenable, since when words such as "fire" (*vahni*) are uttered...

If it is argued that this is not so because it would result in the burning of the mouth and other such consequences, we say no; for it has been stated in the *Tantravārttika* and other works that the word possesses a power (*śakti*) even with respect to its own form. And it was said by Bhartṛhari:
"Just as light possesses two powers—being the object of perception and being the perceiver—"
In the same way, these [phonemes] exist separately from all words.

Thus, for this very reason, the modern grammarians (śābdika-navya) maintain that the identity (*tādātmya*) between word and meaning is itself the expressive power (*śakti*); this is explained in detail elsewhere. And in this way, the meaning of the mantra begins with "having the form of the phonemes *ka*, etc.
Since the nature of the sound itself is described here as the meaning, this is a case where the meaning consists of the form of the sound.
It is designated. || 110 ||

Now, he states the meaning of a portion of the names: "Auspicious One, She of the Single Syllable, Sovereign, and also Lalitā"—in this way, the meaning expressed by each syllable is contained within the three hundred names. (111)

Since it is established in common worldly usage that a name is understood by the mention of even a single part of it, the meaning of a partial name is said to be cognizable through the presentation of the name itself. (112)

For here, by means of the passage beginning with "The auspicious one whose form is the letter Ka," twenty names are stated for each syllable of the fifteen-syllable mantra, starting from the first syllable; these amount to three hundred. And those...

These [explanations] are undertaken for the purpose of illuminating the meaning of the syllables of the mantra. Thus, for the letter *ka*, there are twenty meanings, such as "the one whose form is the letter *ka*," "the auspicious one," and "she who possesses auspicious qualities. In the same way, each of the letters beginning with *e* also has twenty distinct meanings.

And since, in all of those cases, the capacity [of the word] is impossible according to the methods of well-known lexicons, grammars, and so forth, the postulation [of such capacity] must rely on *arthāpatti* (presumption) by the force of this very [text];
and because *arthāpatti*— which consists in the impossibility of [the fact] otherwise— is the principle that "one mentions the whole name by mentioning a part of the name."

Because they are thoroughly examined through reasoning, it is concluded that the letters beginning with *ka* are merely portions of those names. For this very reason, the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda clearly stated that the extracted syllables such as *Śiva*, *Śakti*, and *Kāma* constitute parts of the name.
"O Mother, those castes (varṇas) partake in being components of Your name," so it is said in the *Saundaryalaharī*.

Indeed, there is the practice of denoting a whole by a part, as seen in examples such as "Bhīma" for Bhīmasena, "Satyā" for Satyabhāmā, and "Guru" or "Laghu" for the syllables *ga* and *la*, respectively; this occurs in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter and in the *Yajñāyajñīya* chant.
Expressions such as "udgīthopāntyam," "gāyatrīṣu," "jarābodhīye," "rathantare," "pratihārādiḥ" (to be stated) [for the *iṣṭubh*],
"jñīye," "gīthopāntyam," "trīṣu," "bodhīye," "tare," and "hārādiḥ" are frequently encountered among the Sāmavedins and in the *Phullasūtra*.

And in that regard, since names beginning with the letter *ka* are infinite, and because the letter *ka* itself would thus possess infinite meanings, this very rule is established: "these alone are the meanings, and no others. Furthermore, among those [names], for each syllable of the initial names, by means of both the meaning of the name and the form of the word...

Due to the avoidance of redundancy, only nineteen topics are intended here; thus, even the meaning of the first part of the name becomes nineteenfold. And herein, among the sets of twenty [topics] numbered fifteen, having set aside the first names...
The second names have been set forth, because the first names were obtained through the description of their previous meanings. || 111, 112 ||

Furthermore, regarding these twenty meanings, there is no fixed rule that when describing the meaning of the letter *ka* as "having the form of *ka*," the meaning of the letter *e* must be described as "having the form of *e*," or the meaning of the letter *ī* as "having the form of *ī*."
Since it is also easily stated that the single-syllable mantra in the form of the letter *ka* bestows desired objects,
one should write fifteen syllables here, place the number twenty above each syllable, and upon their mutual multiplication, whatever the resulting number is at the final syllable—
He states that very [result] which is accomplished:
"The meanings of a name arise from its conjunction with a portion of the name, numbering [in order] fifteen, ten, seven, eight, six, four, three, two, one, and zero. (113)
Then, from the combination of the name of the third alternative among the meanings of the names— which consists of a single part of the meaning of a name— and the nineteen-fold [meaning],
multiplied according to the stated method by the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), there follows the subsequent group of dots (*bindu*) which is measured and equalized by that number.

Regarding "those beginning with elephants": eight elephants (*gaja*), six tastes (*rasa*), seven mountains (*giri*), two *dasras*, and three *rāmas*. According to the rule that "the movement of numbers is from left to right," one should first write fifteen dots and then, moving to the left, write the elephants and the others, since the direction is from left to right.
Because the left side itself is the "upper" (uttara).

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: those [entities] such as the elephant and so forth, for whom the group of dots (*bindu-gaṇa*) is upper; having drawn the elephant and others in a counter-clockwise direction, the collection of numbers (*aṅka-samūha*) produced therefrom is subsequently [drawn] in a clockwise direction alone.
There is no dispute regarding the fact that the bindus (zeroes) must be written in this context; and thus,
there are thirty-three hundred and twenty-seven parārdhas (units of ten to the fifty-first power),
six intermediate, and eight final [positions], which constitute the three hundred aforementioned varieties of meaning.

In numerical figures, this is 32,768,000,000,000,000,000. The method for understanding these numbers follows the convention that starting from the final digit, each preceding digit is ten times greater than the one following it. This rule is stated in the *Līlāvatī*:
Eleven, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million, and ten-million [are the units] in successive order;
from that [come] billion (*arbuda*), ten-billion (*abja*), hundred-billion (*kharva*), trillion (*nikharva*), ten-trillion (*mahāpadma*), and hundred-trillion (*śaṅku*).
The ocean (jaladhi), the end (anta), the middle (madhya), and the supreme half (parārdha) are the designations for numbers increasing tenfold at each step.
Thus [ends the section]. Furthermore, the detailed expansion of these numerical figures has been elaborated by us in the eighth chapter of the *Chandaḥkaustubha*. 113.
Now, the meaning of the term *śākā* is twofold: the meaning of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) and the meaning of the aggregate of its powers (*śaktisamūhārtha*).
Among these, the "meaning of the constituent parts" refers to the description of the limbs of the Goddess. As it is said:
"The body of the Mother is [composed] limb by limb through the *kūṭas* of Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti."
In this context, the object to be conveyed extends from the throat, or from the middle, down to the tips of the feet.
In this context, by means of the *vāk-kūṭa* within the *vidyā*, the body is to be established part by part, beginning from the crown and extending down to the throat;
by means of the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, the body from below the throat to the waist is established; and by means of the *śakti-kūṭa*...

The meaning is that the body, extending from the hips down to the tips of the feet, is what is to be presented. For this very reason, with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, it is said in the *Sahasranāma*:
"O you whose lotus-face is the singular essence of the venerable *vāgbhava-kūṭa*."
She has the form of a central peak extending from below the throat to the waist.
She who dwells upon the lower part of the waist that has attained oneness with the Śakti-kūṭa,
whose essence is the root mantra, and whose body consists of the three root-kūṭas.
Thus [ends the verse]. 114.
He states the meaning of the collection of powers (śaktis):
"One should understand the meanings of the six letters ending in 'ra' in their respective order as Brahmā and Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, and Rudra and Pārvatī. (115)
Here, the letters *ha* and *ra* are counted separately, because they are recited in that very manner in specific vidyās such as the Durvāsā-vidyā. || 115 ||
All these, without exception, are indeed the arts of desire (kāmakalā) and none other than that;
this meaning is conveyed by the use of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the suffix -īka. || 116 ||

These six are Brahmā and the others. Although Brahmā and the rest are masculine while Bhāratī and the others are feminine, and thus according to the rule *pumān striyā* (a masculine word remains when combined with a feminine one) under the heading of *ekaśeṣa*, the form should have been *ete* (these); nevertheless—
This statement is made for the purpose of recalling the fact that the female form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara was described in the section concerning the meaning of the word *bhāva*;
[this is known] from their grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in their having the same case-ending. [This applies] to every syllable.
However, there is the elision of existing case-endings (*sup*). Because the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is not intended in a sentence, there is no sandhi with the vowel *ī*. || 116 ||
This very same meaning applies to the other two peaks as well;
however, in the third [peak], the second of the second *hakāras* precedes the *sakāra*.
It must be analyzed letter by letter because it is to be contemplated by those possessing power (*śākta*);
since it is stated to consist of the powers such as Vāmā and Icchā, this is the meaning of the Śākta school. || 118 ||
Whatever meaning belongs to the first peak (kūṭa) is exactly the same for the second and third peaks.
In the second peak, however, the middle *ha*-kāra is suitable for connection with the first part of the third peak; even though it occupies the fourth position there, [it connects].
The expression is used in that way because it is the second among its own class (sajātīya). Therefore, for each of those two *kūṭas* as well, there are exactly six letters ending in the letter *ra*;
thus, their meaning is described according to the method already stated. Here, the power (*śakti*) resides in each individual letter; by means of that—

The meaning of syllables that possess power is "śaktārtha. The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Alternatively, it is the meaning or purpose of those who possess power (*śāktānām upāsakānām arthaḥ prayojanam*). Or else, it is so called because the collection of powers (*śakti-samūha*) is expounded therein; thus there are three etymological explanations. As for the avoidance of redundancy with the word *bhārtha*, [it is as follows]:
It was already done previously. || 117, 118 ||
Now, for the sake of [explaining] *sāmarasya* (homogeneity), he says:
The meanings of the two letters *ka* and *la* are Śiva and Śakti; the meaning of the two pure vowels (*a*) is Śakti.
The state of homogeneity (*samarasa-bhāva*) of both is the *Hṛllekhā*, which is the Supreme Brahman. (119)
"Brahmā alone is Śiva and Śakti"—this is the meaning of each individual peak (kūṭa).
Through the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti, this is the meaning of the equilibrium of Vidyā. || 120 ||

In the *Kādividyā*, there are three *ka*s and two *ha*s; their meaning is Śiva alone. Likewise, there are three *la*s and two *sa*s; their meaning is Śakti. For this very reason, there is a union of *ka* and *la* in the seed-syllable of Manmatha (*klīm*), and a union of *ha* and *sa* in the Parā-prāsāda (*hsauḥ*).
The power (*śakti*) resides in the second and third vowels, *a* and *u*, which are pure.
The meaning of the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*) is the Supreme Brahman, consisting of the equilibrium of both.
[This is formed] by means of the void (*vyoma*), fire (*agni*), the fourth vowel (*turīyasvara*), and the bindu, respectively.

In the commentary on the one hundred and forty-sixth verse, the meaning is that [she] has attained identity with the state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) consisting in the swallowing of light, which is of the single nature of the Supreme Brahman.
Because it will be clarified later: the meaning of each *kuṭa* is that both Śiva and Śakti are Brahman alone. As it is said in the *Triśatikā*:
"The three *ka*s and the two *ha*s are proclaimed as the Śaiva portion."
The remaining syllables are those of power, while the syllable *hrīṃ* is of both natures.
Thus [ends the section]. 119, 120.
Now he states the collective meaning:

from the verbal root *kan*, meaning "to shine," the letter *ka* signifies luminosity; from the root *iṅ*, meaning "to study," the vowel *e* arises, signifying the instrument for that [luminosity]. (121)
The meaning is that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the illuminator through the union of two phonemes.
From the verbal root *ī*, meaning "to pervade," its pervasion constitutes the meaning of the third phoneme. || 122 ||
The abundance of its waves is its manifestation; this is the meaning of the letter *ma*.

That by which something is measured (*kanyate*) or revealed (*prakāśyate*) is "the revealer" (*kaṃ*). The elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) occurs by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), or else the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rule "from roots ending in *ñam*, the suffix *ḍa*. When the root *iṅ* (in the sense of studying) is applied, [it forms *kaṃ*].

Even when *kittva* applies, the *guṇa* [substitution] occurs; it must be made into *vij*. That by which one studies is the instrument of study, namely, the intellect (*buddhi*). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. The absence of *saṃdhi* is an archaic Vedic feature (*ārṣa*). Then, by means of the vowel *ī*, the genitive case ending is elided. In the word *laharī*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. [The form arises] from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*), with the suffix *kvip*.

By applying the rule *tallpe prātipadikādhātvarthe bahulamiṣṭhavat* [Pāṇini 5.3.56] and the rule *ṇeraniṭi* [Pāṇini 6.4.51] for the elision of the *ṇic*-suffix, the form *m* is established. Its nature is that of illuminating and subtlety. Thus, the meaning of the first *kūṭa* is the excellence of subtle pervasiveness. || 121, 122 ||
The syllable *haṃ* signifies valor, because it is the instrument for slaying adversaries; [the root] *han* means "to kill. ||123||
Wealth is the means for enjoyment, derived from the roots *syati* (to pour forth) or *sunoti* (to press out);
while "the desirable" (*kama*) refers to women and the like, which are the objects of desire, derived from the root *kam* (to love). 124.
The "going" (gamana) of these [waves] is that which arises from a verbal root (*dhātu*) meaning motion (*gati*) with the prefix *pra* and the suffix *aṇ*;
its excellence (*atiśaya*) is the "wave" (*laharī*), which is here [phonetically] fused by means of *savaraṇadīrgha* [vowel lengthening]. || 125 ||
The letter *ī* signifies his fame, because it shines in all directions;
this is derived from the verbal root *īḍ*, "to shine," while the meaning of the letter *m* in these two [names] is as follows. || 126 ||

*Haṃ* means valor (*śaurya*), derived from the root *han* (to strike), according to the rule *hanyate 'neneti haṃ*. The elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) occurs by the rule *anudāttopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikalopo jhalikṅiti*. From the roots *ṣo* (in the sense of ending) or *ṣuñ* (in the sense of distilling), with the suffix *ḍa* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the form *sam* is obtained. It is that by which one is bound (*sīyate*) or produced (*sūyate*).
Or "saṃ" refers to substance (*dravya*). "Kaṃ" is that which is desired, such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth.

There is a *dvandva* compound of the [words] beginning with "ha. Then, with the letter "ha," which signifies attainment, there is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Then, with the word "laharī," there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Finally, with the vowel "ī," [there is another compound].

There is a *dvandva* compound with the word meaning "fame" (*kīrti*), followed by a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the letter *ma*. Thus, the meaning of the second *kūṭa* is the creation of fame characterized by the excellence of attaining valor, wealth, and women. (123–126)
He states that very point first:
the meaning of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa is the excellence of subtle intellect and pervasiveness;
the meaning of the Kāmarāja is the excellence of valor, wealth, women, and fame. || 127 ||
This is clear. || 127 ||
One who correctly understands all these [letters] becomes "Hṛ" from the root *hṛ* (to seize);
the meaning of that letter is "the one who withdraws the entire world. 128.
The vowel *ī* is joined [to the preceding consonant] and signifies the agent who illuminates the forms of creation and maintenance;
or rather, because she shines in the heart removing all distress, she is the Mother (*mātā*) of *hrī*. 129.
A *karmadhāraya* compound should be formed with the word ending in "sakala" and the syllable "hrīṃ";
its substantive would be "maḥ," meaning either the *syānāda* (the primordial sound) or consciousness (*saṃvit*). || 130 ||

The *dvandva* compound of the two *kūṭas*. She who perfectly fashions these in emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is *sakalā*; there is an elision of the letter *m*. That which takes away is *hṛ*. From the verbal root *ī* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*), *ī* means radiance. Radiance consists of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthiti*). When *hṛ* and *ī* are combined as a *karmadhāraya* and the *yaṇ*-sandhi is applied, it becomes *hrī*.

The meaning is that she is characterized as the performer of the fivefold cosmic functions, beginning with creation (*sṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, *hṛ* means "she takes" or "she makes everything her object"; [the suffix] *kvip* is applied. Because the rules governing augments (*āgama*) are not mandatory, there is no insertion of *tuk* in this instance.
That is the *daharākāśa* (the small ether). She shines therein; thus she is *hrīḥ*. This refers to the word ending in *hrī*.

The compound *karmadhāraya* is formed with the letter *ma*. Although the letter *ma* does not exist at all within the three *kūṭas*, because it is the *anusvāra* alone that is extracted in the tantras, nevertheless, by virtue of the definition of the *makara*, it is easy to say that the *anusvāra* [is present] in the two *kūṭas*; however, this is not so in the final *kūṭa*.

Let it be that only the anusvāra remains as the remainder. Consequently, the meaning of the mantra is established as follows: Brahman is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), in the form of sound (nāda) residing within the small ether (daharākāśa), the creator of the abundance of intellect, heroism, wealth, women, and fame, and the creator of the entire universe and so forth.

And this matter has been explained in detail by the venerable commentators (*bhāṣyakāras*), who demonstrated the application of the *Brahmasūtras* according to their inherent power (*śakti*); here it is stated in brief. In certain places therein, an apparent contradiction with grammar is perceived, and that—

Since the authority of the mantra and the meaning of the mantra is established by virtue of their having been proclaimed by seers (*ṛṣi*), and because it has been said that "grammarians rely upon usage," the grammatical definitions must be formulated in accordance with this very principle; thus [any objection] is to be set aside. (128–130)
He demonstrates that very manner [of formation]:

"Because the verbal root has multiple meanings, because of the inclusion of the term *bahula*, because it belongs to the *pṛṣodara*-class, through its recitation in the *ākṛtigaṇa* [list], and by the postulation of *uṇādi* suffixes according to one's own preference. (131)
Since all grammatical rules in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) are optional, this point has been established by Manu;
regarding this matter thus set forth, we grant our approval to the instruction of the grammarians.

In the rule *kurdakhurdagurdaguda krīḍāyām eva*, the word *eva* (only) [indicates that these roots mean only "to play"]; and because of the force of the specification of meaning in the rule *takṣas tanūkaraṇe* ("*takṣ* means 'to shape'"), the specification of meanings such as "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth is merely illustrative; thus, verbal roots have multiple meanings. Therefore—
Even though the root *syati* denotes the completion of an action (*antakarman*), its meaning of "enjoyment" (*upabhoga*) is not contradictory. For this very reason,

although the root *iṭ* cannot be used in isolation because it is preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the vowel *ī* itself— contained within the group *iṭ-kiṭa-kaṭī* in the sense of "motion"— will serve as the carrier of this meaning, since roots signifying motion [can convey various nuances].
Because all [grammatical rules] have knowledge as their purpose. Regarding the term *bāhulaka*:
in some cases there is application, in some cases non-application, in some cases optionality, and in some cases something entirely different.
Having observed the various modes of prescription for a rule, this fourfold variety is called *bāhulaka*.
They say.

Thus, the meaning of the term *bahulapada* is established. By this, the elision of the vowel *a* in *lahrī* is accomplished. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing forms such as *raṇḍaḥ*, the fact that the suffix *ḍa* following a root ending in a nasal (*ñam*) is itself marked with the *ḍit* designation is also established. He states another alternative: "because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. According to the rule, "words such as *pṛṣodara* are as they are taught [in usage]."
The meaning is that words such as *pṛṣodara* are correct exactly as they are employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*);
no further grammatical rule need be sought for them. Nor does this imply that the form *lahrī* would also result as a usage in other instances, just like the word *pṛṣodara*.

It must be stated that this is because the rule "the suffix *sa* is applied here alone" has been accepted. For this very reason, the term *gūḍhātmā* is not employed in other contexts. And for this same reason, in the *Viṣṇusahasranāmabhāṣya*, regarding the passage "Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha," it is stated that the sandhi [elision] occurs by virtue of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda says: regarding the absence of [the word] *gaṇa* in the list of nominal stems (*gaṇapāṭha*), he states "ākṛti" and so forth. Since the suffix *ḍa* is not seen after the root *ṣuñ*, he says "svecchā" and so forth. In technical names (*saṃjñā*), the forms of roots and the suffixes following them [are used].
One should understand the consequence from the action; this is the instruction taught in the scriptures.

The meaning is that, because of this statement, the designation *ḍit* is postulated for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* suffix. He states "in Vedic usage" (*chandasīti*) to show that the resolution by appealing to the Vedic character (*chāndasatva*) is unrestrained. || 131, 132 ||
He concludes by first providing an etymological explanation of all the constituent words:

"Because it involves numerous compounding, because it is stated to be the means for accomplishing all human goals, and because its essence is stated in brief, this Śrīvidyā contains the meaning of everything. (133)

The etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is either "the meaning of the whole compound," or "that in which all (*samasta*)—meaning complete—objects (*artha*), that is, the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), reside," or "the summarized meaning. || 133 ||
Now, he states the meaning with its qualities: "Ka" is the rule, "e" is Hari, and "a" is Īśa; for the purpose of praise, the word "īḍa" is used.
For the letter "ḍa" situated between two vowels, "la" is the substitute. (134)
By this, the nature of the first peak as the Ṛgveda is indicated;
through that same sequence, the status of the subsequent pair of peaks as the Yajurveda and Sāmaveda is established. || 135 ||

The word *hrīm* is the specific name, neuter in gender, as it characterizes Brahman; "Brahman, who is praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva"—this is the meaning of the first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*). || 136 ||
The letter *e* is joined with the preceding form, the letter *a*;

and that [letter *a*] denotes Śiva, according to the lexicon which states: "The letter *a* [denotes] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Kamaṭha. Since it is stated that "Ka is declared to be Prajāpati," the letter *e* is said to denote Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, the *k* and *e* [of *eka*] refer to Brahmā and Viṣṇu as stated in the *Ekākṣaranighaṇṭu*.

Regarding the root *īḍ* (to praise), in the sense of "one who is to be praised" (*stutya*), because this [deity] consists of the letter *a*, there is a substitution of *l* for the letter *ḍ* situated between the two *a*s,
as in the mantra *agnirmūrdhā divaḥ kakut*.

This is stated in the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya*: "When this [ḍakāra] comes between two vowels, it becomes the letter *la*. And this very [rule] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the first *kūṭa* consists of the *Ṛgveda*.

Regarding the fact that the second and third *kūṭas* consist of the Yajurveda and Sāmaveda respectively: although in the verse "Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi," the letter *la* alone was extracted by the word "Vajrapāṇi" and not the letter *la*, this is nevertheless intended on the basis of the non-difference between *la* and *la*. For this very reason...

In some tantras, all three [letters] belonging to the *trikhaṇḍa* are indeed extracted by the term *mohārṇa* (the syllable of delusion), which refers to the letter *la*. As for the term "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*), it is more appropriate to consider it an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *svarādi* (a class of indeclinables). For this very reason, in the *Triśatikā*, regarding the ninety-ninth name...
Even when the fourth case ending is required for the word *namaḥ*, the traditional usage of the masters, *hrīṃ namaḥ*, is thus justified. (134–136)

*Hasaka* is considered to mean "one with a laughing face," because the letter *ka* denotes the face. Alternatively, *hasa* means bliss (*ānanda*), *ka* means the sun, and *ha* would be the moon. || 137 ||
That which has these two as its eyes is called *kahala-ravindu-netra*. By this, its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatva*) is declared, owing to its quality of illumination. || 138 ||
These two—having a smiling face (*hasatva*) and being the *ha* vowel—are the reasons for being worshiped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
therefore, "the Consciousness-Brahman is unsurpassed bliss" is the meaning of the second *kūṭa*. || 139 ||

*Hasa* means laughter (*hāsya*). The suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group. Then, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the letter *ka*, which denotes the mouth. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose *hasa* (laughter) is *ka* (the mouth). Alternatively, since laughter is produced by bliss (*ānanda*), the word *hasa* is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) for bliss; thus, *hasa* and *ka* [refer to bliss and the mouth].

"Tell me, tell me: that which is spoken by 'ka' is 'kahala' (the sun). What is remembered for 'ha' in the mouth, the sun, anger, Varuṇa, the moon, and Indra? And 'la' shall be in the eye. This is the *Ekākṣaranighaṇṭu* (Glossary of Single Syllables).
There is a *karmadhāraya* compound between the words *hasa* and *padakahala*. [This is] the elucidation of this meaning.
He states the root [mantra]: "The causes" (hetū). Since it is *hrīṃ hasakahalaṃ*, the sequence is therefore *hrīṃ ka e ī laṃ*. (137–139)
The meaning of the third peak (kūṭa) is indeed the Brahman accompanied by all its parts (sakala) along with all the arts (kalās).
Thus, through the description of the multitude of qualities, this is the qualified (saguṇa) meaning of the Vidyā. || 140 ||
In all these cases, there is elision of the *su* suffix; the rest is clear. || 140 ||
He states the meaning of the Great Saying (mahāvākya) indicated last:
"The words for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are also the letter *ka*, the letter *e*, and the letter *a*;
they are indicative (lākṣaṇika) of their respective functions as the generators of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (141)
The letter *ī* signifies Īśvara, and the letter *ḍ* signifies Sadāśiva;
by means of these two, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the functions of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*) are expressed therein. (142)

The letter *ī* denotes Īśvara by the principle of denoting a whole through a part of its name. Furthermore, although there is the statement, "Ḍa is declared to be Maheśa," in the present context, Sadāśiva alone is intended as the bestower of grace (*anugraha*). By this, that which is stated in such Vedic passages as, "From whence indeed these beings are born," and so forth, [is explained].
Thus, the incidental definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) of Brahman has been stated. || 141, 142 ||
Now, with the second *kūṭa*, he states the definition of the essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite":
*ha* is bliss (*ānanda*), *sa* is truth (*satya*), *ka* is happiness (*ka*), *ha* is the infinite (*ananta*), and *la* is knowledge (*jñāna*).
According to the lexicon (*kośa*), the letter *ka* denotes a "friend" (*sakhi*) in the phrase "What is called a friend by the wise?

Friendliness (*sakhitva*) is trustworthiness (*āptatva*), and that consists in speaking according to reality; thus, through a relationship of capability (*śakyasaṃbandha*), it is "truth" (*satya*) itself that is intended in the present context. Likewise, because the letter *ha* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of space (*vyoman*).
The meaning is that it is infinite because space is infinite;
the word *lakāra*, which denotes the eye that produces perceptual knowledge, has "knowledge" as its referent. || 142 ||
Thus, having determined Brahman by means of the pair of definitions—the incidental (taṭastha) and the essential (svarūpa)—[the author proceeds]. || 143 ||

He declares the non-difference [of the Self] within the multitude of living beings by means of the third peak-syllable, due to its association with the triad of phases known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (144)
The entire phrase consists of the term for the individual soul (jīva) and the term for the Supreme Brahman, which is the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), its meaning is the non-difference between the two pure entities indicated by those terms. || 145 ||
What has been stated is too little; in order to enlighten [the disciple] that "all this, indeed, is Brahman," the entire word [Brahman] is employed, situated within the third peak-syllable.

Thus, having described the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman through intermediate sentences, their non-difference has been expounded; this is the meaning of the great primary statement. || 147 ||

In the great sentence *tattvamasi* ("That thou art"), non-difference is understood through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in the two words— the referent of *tat* and the referent of *tvam*— possessing the same case-ending; and this [non-difference] is [understood] through the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the "renouncing-non-renouncing" indication), since it is impossible for the primary literal meanings [of those two terms] to be identical.

Such is the established rule regarding the relationship between the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) and the literal meaning (*vācya*). In this context, the literal meaning of the word *tat* (That) is the generator of the fivefold cosmic functions, such as creation and so forth; and that [meaning] is described by the passage beginning with, "From which indeed these beings are born."
It is stated in the Śruti: "The indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha), however, is Brahman, which is beyond all action and devoid of distinctions;

that too has been established by such passages as 'Truth, Knowledge,' and so forth. Thus, the denoted meaning (vācyārtha) of the term *tvam* is characterized by the five states beginning with waking, and it is just as in this space.
"Just as a hawk or a falcon, having flown around and become weary, folds its wings and holds itself steady for the sake of alighting, even so does this living being hasten toward that end.
This is stated in such scriptural passages as, "Just as a great fish," and so forth.

The indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), however, is Brahman, which transcends all states [of being]. That too has been established by such passages as, "This person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart," and "One should not see the seer of seeing."
Thus, when the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) have been determined through these intermediate sentences,

there arises, within the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the realization of the non-difference between the two indicated meanings. Although in the Śrutis only the three functions and the three states are described, nevertheless, in accordance with the Tantras—

This should be explained as being intended to indicate those five, just as the process of "trivṛtkaraṇa" (threefold-making) is intended to indicate "pañcīkaraṇa" (fivefold-making). And thus, in the present context, although the literal meaning has been stated by the word *sakala* ("with all") situated in the third peak— which signifies "accompanied by the *kalās* and the *avasthās*,"— even so...

Because the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) has not been stated, there is a deficiency; to remedy this, the two peaks [of the mountain] must be explained by repeating them as the providers of both the denoted meaning (vācyārtha) and the indicated meaning for the term *tvaṃ*.
Alternatively, according to the view of the Tantrikas, there is an absolute non-difference even between the two denoted meanings.

Since this has been established by the authors of the *Śāmbhavānandakalpalatā* and other works, the two *kūṭas* convey the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) as qualified by the agency of creation and so forth, or indeed as qualified by the various states;
whereas in the third *kūṭa*, there is the non-duality of those two, or the non-duality of the entire universe.
It is explained: here, having stated as much of the subject matter as needs to be said, we desist, lest the entire Vedānta-śāstra itself would have to be commenced [again].
Regarding the term *mahāpūrva*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both great (*mahān*) and prior (*pūrvaḥ*)"—thus the word *mahā*.
Alternatively, the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is that the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is that which is [expressed] by the word at its beginning.
These meanings are illustrative; therefore, they include other meanings mentioned here and there in the Tantras. For instance, in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

Beginning with "One should perceive the vibration of the Self; that is the supreme *kalā*," and after stating four groups of four categories each, the expressive nature of the four words— the three *kūṭas* and the fourth *vidyā*— has been established.
Furthermore, for the entire mantra endowed with the three peaks (kūṭas),
these forms of the expressed meaning consist of the Kula and Kaula principles.
Thus, there are as many meanings of the mantra as there are sets of four. And these are stated in the first section in the verse beginning with "puṭadhāma" (the abode of the folds).

For although in that context the non-difference of the *kūṭas* from the folds and so forth is indeed mentioned, nevertheless, that [relationship] is precisely the relation between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

It culminates [in this], because it has been very clearly established in both the *Pātañjala-mañjūṣā* and elsewhere that the identity (*tādātmya*) between word and meaning itself constitutes the nature of the expressive power (*śakti*). Likewise, in the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Kādimata*, by means of three disordered syllables beginning with the twenty-fourth [letter].

The meaning has been described by means of verses: "By those [verses] which have been composed, the meaning of the three worlds has been made clear; through their form, the supreme state will be attained. (1)
May he who has drawn the furrows for the ploughing of the field at the very beginning,
and who is the Lord of the Tīrtha, protect us from all sides in our bodies and in our offspring.

You are the one to be questioned regarding the recitation of the Kāma-mantras; you are not [subject to] the fire-offering, O Agni; you are the one who has shaken off the body of the hundred-fold [sacrificial] vessel.
Thus it is said. The sequence for reciting these is as follows:
"devatārathagomūka" (84627351). He who does not know this sequence is mute regarding the scrambled syllables, even though he may be a "devatārathaga."
Thus, by the three syllables of Lalitā, the entire meaning is expressed;
by the remainder, which is the form of the Goddess herself, this [text] is said to have been uttered. (1)
The entire world in its entirety is said to consist of the mental impression (hṛllekhā);
its meaning, however, has been declared as that which is hidden in all the Tantras. (2)
The state of being illuminated by the void (*vyoman*) and the state of devouring by fire (*agni*);

the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of these two is the letter *ī*, and its contemplation is by means of the *bindu*. (3) In the third *kūṭa*, the three phonemes signify all things, while the fourth syllable signifies the Goddess. Therefore, this is the meaning:

The meaning of the first verse is "accomplished" (saṃpanna). The meaning of the second verse—that the entire world is indeed the form of the Goddess—is concealed in other tantras. That which is illuminating by means of the four syllables residing in the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjābīja)—

And that which devours [objects]—the state of equilibrium between those two—is their identity (*tādātmya*), which is established in the second [chapter]; thus, it belongs to the third. Furthermore, the terms "light" (*prakāśa*) and "devouring" (*grāsa*) are designations for emergence and dissolution, or for knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). This is also the meaning.
This has been stated as being too brief in the verse beginning with *sūcitaḥ*. Thus, in this context,
within the thirteen meanings of the verse beginning with *puṭadhāma*,
there are four meanings pertaining to the inner essence (*bhāvārtha*), three meanings pertaining to names (*nāmārtha*), and two meanings pertaining to power (*śāktārtha*).

Regarding the meaning of *kaulika*, there are three types based on the distinctions of the Goddess (*devī*), the Vidyā, and the Cakra; regarding the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), there are two types. Thus, fourteen [meanings] plus the remaining ten, totaling thirty-seven meanings. However, regarding the meaning of a portion of a name, the divisions are infinite.
Thus it has been stated. In this manner, other meanings as well may be gathered by those who have studied many tantras.

Whatever meanings have been shown by Manoratha, whether through direct denotation (śakti) or through indication (lakṣaṇā), there is no dispute regarding them, because they are established by direct perception itself.

Regarding the mantra "manomantra": the phrase "by direct perception" (pratyakṣeṇa) means that the grammar, lexicons, and other means of grasping the expressive power (śakti), as well as the relationship between the signifier and the signified (śakyasaṃbandha), are clearly demonstrated; this is the intended meaning. || 148 ||
Furthermore, regarding those six meanings—beginning with "existence" (bhāva)—which were stated by Manu:
even if power (śakti) and devotion (bhakti) are not possible among them, what loss is there? (149)

Because there is an absence of grammar and other means for apprehending *śakti*, there is no *śakti*; for this very reason, there is also no *bhakti* (secondary signification) in the form of a relationship with the denotable. There will be a third function (*vṛtti*) in the form of manifestation (*vyakti*), [arising] from the speaker, the person to be addressed, intonation (*kāku*), the proximity of others, and the expressed meaning itself.

With the intention that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "due to the excellence of the introductory context, place, time, and so forth, for those possessed of intuitive insight" (*pratibhājuṣām*) will also include "devotional practice" (*upāsanā*), he provides the following resolution: "What loss [is there]? (149).

Since many do not accept the theory of *vyañjanā* (suggestion), he says: "Let other distinct modes of operation be set aside; however, the apprehension of that [meaning] shall occur through the mind by virtue of Śiva’s word—let this indeed be the power (*śakti*) itself. (150)

This meaning is to be understood from this [text], because it is the will of the Lord (Īśvara). It is "other," being distinct from power (*śakti*), devotion (*bhakti*), and manifestation (*vyakti*); that is, it possesses a process distinct from the threefold process beginning with power. Abandoning the path of the unrestrained, he says:

Or rather, the sense is that this meaning belongs to [the text] by Śiva himself, because it has been clearly stated as such. (150) Even if there is ignorance regarding the specific meaning of every single word, let alone [the meaning of] an indivisible sentence. (151)
For it is the established doctrine that the referent (artha) is also of an indivisible nature and distinct from the qualified [cognition];
let it even possess the status of a word, like such terms as "āsecanaka" or "vyāpti. 152.

In the present context, because the word itself becomes an object [of the desire] by virtue of possessing a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) as determined by a modehood (prakāratā) residing in the capacity to produce the understanding of the meaning— [as expressed in the desire]: "May this word bring about the understanding of this meaning."
If it is argued that there can be no capacity [to convey meaning] because the meaning is not expressed by each individual word (*pratipada*), we say no;

for we postulate an intention (*icchā*) precisely in the form: "Let this sentence convey this indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārtha*). That a sentence is indivisible is indeed accepted by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

The indivisibility of the referent (*artha*) is indeed desired by the followers of the Upaniṣads who describe the meaning of such sentences as "the moon is the supreme light. And when this is investigated, it results in the very fact that the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is something distinct [from its qualifiers]. Thus, where...

Regarding the discernment of meaning in each step, this is the method: wherever that [meaning] is not present, let there be only the status of a single word for the complete [expression]. Nor should it be argued that the capacity of a single word to denote multiple distinct meanings is unobserved; for such cases are indeed seen.
Because the pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), the pot (*ghaṭa*), and the inherence in the pot (*ghaṭasamavāya*) are all denotable by the word "pot" (*ghaṭapadavācyatvāt*);
and because of the lexicon (*kośa*) stating that "that which is *asecanaka* is such that there is no end to one's satisfaction from seeing it";

and [because of the definition of pervasion as] the non-counterpositiveness of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāvāpratiyogitva*) residing in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as the reason (*hetu*), with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*).

And because the word *karaṇya* has the meaning of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), he says "āsecanaka," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is intended. Therefore, even though the word itself is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in the case of the Lord's will, there is no contingency of postulating a distinct kind of will for the sake of establishing the present context. —151, 152—
Now, one might object that if this [word] is a single word, the fault of having multiple meanings would follow; to this he says:
"Multiple meanings for a single [word] are observed in cases such as *hari* and *saindhava*;
when only one of these is to be understood, context and intention serve as the differentiators. (153)
In the present case, however, since all cognition is accepted [as the object], we have no expectation for a qualifying attribute.
Alternatively, just as in the case of the word "puṣpavant" (the sun and moon), there is a unity of power regarding all objects here as well. (154)
There is no fault, because the fact that a word has multiple meanings is established by the authority of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In all instances where a word has multiple meanings, the fault of postulating [an additional factor] does not arise, because the knowledge of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth serves as the cause for understanding only one of those meanings; however, in the present case, that [cause] is absent.

Thus he says with the words "anyatama" and so forth. Alternatively, just as in the case of the sun and the moon, only one single sufficient denotedness (*viśeṣyatā*) belonging to the cognition that has become the object of God’s will is accepted, so too there is no multiplicity of powers (*śakti*) in the word *puṣpavanta*.
He says "or rather" (atha vā) to indicate that it is likewise here as well. || 153, 154 ||
Wherever there is a meaning expressed in every step, let that be a sentence; in some cases, there is a subordinate sentence, a compound sentence, or a great sentence. (155)

In this context, "intermediate sentence" (*avāntaravākya*) refers to [sentences] within the meaning of the *gāyatrī*, the meaning of names, and so forth, as well as within the meaning of the qualities (*saguṇa*), the meaning of the parts (*avayava*), and so on. The nature of being an intermediate sentence consists simply in being a collection of words (*padasamūhatva*), provided that it is distinct from a collection of sentences (*vākyasamūha*). It is not...
Furthermore, in this context, the nature of being qualified by a great sentence (mahāvākya) is as follows:
a compound sentence (samāsavākya) refers to the collective meaning, while a great sentence (mahāvākya) refers to the ultimate meaning. || 155 ||
The multiplicity of meanings [of a word] arises from its application to multiple objects;
this is frequently accepted in the Veda, but here [in grammar], it occurs through application to a single object. (156)
The rule that [the Veda] makes known all objects postulates an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as a restrictive factor;
for once the firmness of its authority is established, everything must indeed be postulated so as not to contradict it.
Just as the fault of having multiple meanings (*anekārthatā*) can be avoided in the case of the *pada*-view, it is likewise possible in the case of the *vākya*-view;

for the Puruṣasūkta is accepted as having multiple meanings due to its application (*viniyoga*) in the worship of various respective deities. However, this is the distinction: in each specific worship...

The meaning is that while there is recollection of each individual object in the *Puruṣasūkta*, in the present context, however, the production of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) occurs precisely through the recollection of all the objects. || 156, 157 ||
Regarding the statement "once [the object] is established, there is firmness of the means of valid cognition," he provides an illustration:

when the causal relationship between a sacrifice and heaven is fully established, the postulation of an extraordinary *apūrva* (unseen force) is made in order to refute its logical inconsistency. || 158 ||

In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," although the third-case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) indicates that the sacrifice is the producer and heaven— being the object of desire— is the produced, these two cannot be related as cause and effect because they exist at different times; therefore, [the result arises] through such factors as the grace of the deity or the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the sacrifice.
"Because there is no other way to account for it, the impossibility [of the ritual action] is dispelled by the apūrva alone"—such is the detailed explanation in other Tantras. || 158 ||
In this section, he summarizes and restates the fifteen topics previously described: the science, the number of phonemes, the extraction [of mantras], the time, and their pronunciation.
That is the place of arising; effort is the place of abiding of form. || 159 ||
The *ākāra* (form) is its own nature (*svarūpa*), the object (*artha*) to be meditated upon, and the internal limbs (*antaraṅga*).
In the context of the Vidyā, the number of phonemes (*varṇasaṃkhyā*) consists of fifty-eight forms.
The extraction (*uddhāra*) is stated as beginning with "Krodhīśa mounted upon Śrīkaṇṭha," and so forth.

The duration of *vidyā* consists of twenty-nine measures minus one *lava*; the duration of its pronunciation consists of twenty-nine measures minus one *lava*. This has been stated in the three and a half verses beginning with "pronunciation" (*uccāraṇam*) and "thus of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*). Furthermore, the place of origin is in the throat (*kaṇṭhe*).

It has been stated [in the previous section] regarding the throat and palate: "Effort is both external and internal"; "the triad beginning with form is like the fire of dissolution," and so forth; "one's own form, through the distinction between the individual and the collective," and so forth;
that which is to be contemplated consists of the five states and so on; [and] the object.
It consists of the meaning and other aspects of the Gāyatrī. Because they are internal, these are absolutely necessary for practitioners. 159, 159.
The seers, the meters, the deities, the applications, the seeds, the powers, and the spikes. (160)
The ritual placements (nyāsa), meditations (dhyāna), observances (niyama), worship (pūjā), and so forth are the external limbs;
these external limbs, moreover, are for the most part similar to what is well-known in the world. || 161 ||

The sages are Hayagrīva and others; the meters are Paṅkti and so forth; the deity is Tripurasundarī; the application is in the production of desired objects; the seed-syllable is Vāgbhava and so forth;
the power is Parā and so forth; the pin is Kāmarāja and so forth; and the ritual placements are the entire network of placements beginning with the sage.
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is described by the passage beginning with "the Dawn [goddess] whose eyes are rippled with compassion," and so forth.

Observances (*niyama*) consist of the resolve to abstain from eating sugarcane stalks and the like. Worships (*pūjā*) are of three kinds—daily (*nitya*) and so forth—and range from the placement of the vessel (*prātrāsādana*) up to the peace-chant (*śāntistava*).

They are also threefold according to the division of *para* and so forth, and fivefold according to the division of *kevala* and so forth. By "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *homa*, *tarpaṇa*, and other rites is intended. These are necessary as external limbs (*bahir-aṅga*). They are of well-known ritual forms (*prasiddha-kalpa*), meaning they possess a degree of renown that is slightly less than [the most] established. Generally (*prāyaḥ*).

The meaning is that these are well-known. The suffix *kalpa* is used here. The intention is that since we have already explained those [details] extensively in the *Prakāśavarivasyā-vidhi*, they are not mentioned in this present work. || -160, 161 ||
The internal limb is difficult to attain; therefore, it should generally be honored by those whose minds are turned inward.
Consequently, this secret worship has been prescribed for their satisfaction. 162.

"By people whose minds are turned inward and unattached to sense-objects, [the two sciences] were pointed out and instructed on the path of the two knowledges as taught by the sages"—this is according to the usage of Kālidāsa. || 162 ||
Abandoning this [inner practice], the external ritual worship performed by the dull-witted is like a body deprived of life, or like a puppet whose string has snapped. (163)
The meaning is as follows: that [state] in which there is external ostentation and expansion of limbs;

because the vital breath (prāṇa) and the central channel (sūtra) are internal, the sense is that just as those two lack the capacity for action in the absence of such [internal support], so it is here. || 163 ||
From the seed comes the root; from the root come the internal and external expansions of the field.
Although there is equality between these two, nevertheless, the internal one holds primacy.

From the seed—both in the form of the *kāmakalā* and in the form of grain and so forth—the root is the base of the tree and the mantra. This refers to the field, which is both the body and the agricultural plot. Although there is a similarity between these two, as there is no difference in their being produced from a seed.

Nevertheless, the meaning is that while the internal sound perishes when the external branch-bearing tree perishes, even upon the destruction of the external branch alone, there is neither the destruction of the tree nor the destruction of the internal sound; for this is a well-known fact. || 164 ||
Although these [topics] have been included here in this treatise because they are more essential,
he says that acceptance based solely on the power of one's scholarship— by merely looking at this book without depending on a teacher— leads to sin:
This [wisdom], obtained through the grace of the true guru’s lineage, gives birth to all desired goals;
whereas that which is produced by one's own intellect alone brings only evil, like a daughter born of oneself. 165.

"O Sūta, [this is] evil"—thus is the connection. [This refers to those who are devoid of the lineage] of a true Guru, who is characterized by the qualities described in the *Tantrarāja* as "beautiful," "fair-faced," "self-abiding," and so forth. By grace—that is, by the favor born of service—[one attains this, unlike] those who are devoid of the oral tradition and are arrogant merely on account of their knowledge.
Through their violation of the samaya, these mirages manifest as transformations.

According to this statement, "marīcayaḥ" refers to the Ḍākinīs and others. They "vikurvanti," which means they kill by bringing about a transformation of the bodily elements (dhātu). In the case of a maiden, the "good guru" is the father-in-law. || 165 ||

In accordance with the saying, "For scriptures that have auspiciousness at their beginning, auspiciousness in their middle, and auspiciousness at their end become renowned," he composes an auspicious conclusion: "Having attained my own knowledge, which has 'ha' as its distinguishing mark and is beyond description."
Victorious are the feet of the Guru, who gives to me Ānanda, who is indeed my very own. || 166 ||
"Beyond the scope of words" means being outside the domain of speech;

that is to say, transcending the level of what can be expressed. "Ha" indicates certainty. "Containing an interval within its definition" means having a space or occasion for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); in the alternative sense:

The three lines of the triangle situated in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus consist of the three groups of sixteen syllables beginning with A, Ka, and Tha; in the corners within that [triangle] are the three letters beginning with Ha, wherein the meditation upon the Guru is taught in the Tantras.
The meaning is "such a seat"; *māsaka* means non-different from the Self. || 166 ||
Accompanied solely by Gūcarṇa, Bhāskararāya composed the *Varivasyātirahasya*, which is to be revered by heroes, for the Mother of the World. (167)
"By heroes"—meaning by those renowned in the *Parapañcāśikā* and other works for effecting the destruction of this enemy upon the field of battle; thus, everything is faultless. || 167 ||
May that Reality, which is the subject at hand, be established for us— a Reality of incomparable splendor,

which destroys the mass of sins through the removal of the burden of all books held in the hands, and which, being the source of auspiciousness, renders easy the darkness that is otherwise difficult to cross. May it bestow a multitude of blessings.
The pair of fine breasts are the song, the water, and the thunder; they are extolled by Vāstoṣpati.

Thus [ends the work] by the bee at the lotus feet of the venerable Śrī Nṛsiṃhānandanātha— who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences (Padavākyapramāṇa) and is independent in all systems (Sarvatantrasvatantra)—
and who is the son of the venerable Gambhīrarāya Bhāratī Dīkṣita.
The *Varivasyārahasya*, composed with its commentary by Bhāsurānandanātha, also known as Bhāskararāya, is complete.
